For example, the SG cannot order a ceasefire — only the SC can authorize enforcement. This misconception leads to blaming the SG for SC paralysis.
c11_psy_cbse_02_010	Students believe "statistical significance (p < 0.05) means the effect is large, important, or clinically meaningful." They equate p-value with effect size. This error stems from misunderstanding that p-value depends on both effect size AND sample size (p ∝ effect size × √n). Students focus only on the "significant/not significant" binary.
c12_ps_cbse_06_003	Students often believe "veto power means any P5 can stop ANY UNSC decision." The error: veto applies ONLY to substantive matters (Chapter VI pacific settlement, Chapter VII enforcement, admission of new members, Secretary-General appointment). Procedural matters (agenda setting, meeting rules, establishing subsidiary bodies) are decided by 9 affirmative votes — NO veto applies. Example: In 1950, USSR boycotted UNSC over China representation; the Council adopted Resolution 83 (Korea intervention) as a procedural matter without USSR veto. Students who miss this distinction cannot explain why some controversial actions proceed despite P5 opposition.
c11_psy_cbse_02_011	Students believe "ethical research = getting a signed consent form." They treat informed consent as a *one-time event* (signing paper) rather than an *ongoing process* requiring: (1) disclosure of *all* material information (including deception), (2) verification of comprehension (not just signature), (3) freedom from coercion (no grade penalties for refusal), (4) continuous right to withdraw *during* the study. Concrete example: In a board exam answer, a student writes "Participants gave informed consent because they signed the form before the experiment." But the study used deception (told it was a "perception study" but actually measured conformity). The student misses that consent was *not informed* — the participant didn't know the true purpose. This error appears in 60%+ of Class 11 
c12_ps_cbse_06_004	Students often believe "G4 = India + Brazil + Germany + Japan" is a formal treaty bloc like BRICS. In reality, G4 is an *ad hoc coordination group* formed in 2004 solely for UNSC reform; it has no charter, secretariat, or binding commitments. Each member pursues distinct bilateral strategies — e.g., Japan links reform to development aid, Germany to EU coordination, Brazil to South-South leadership. This misconception leads to wrong answers like "G4 jointly vetoes resolutions" or "G4 has a common candidate for Secretary-General." The correct understanding: G4 is a tactical alliance on *one issue only*, dissolving if reform succeeds.
c11_psy_cbse_03_001	Students frequently treat "maturation" and "learning" as synonyms, or assume maturation means "becoming mature" in the colloquial sense (psychological maturity). Specifically, they believe: (1) If a behaviour appears without explicit teaching, it must be maturation (ignoring incidental learning, observational learning, implicit environmental scaffolding); (2) Maturation implies the behaviour is fixed and unmodifiable (ignoring plasticity — NCERT: "proficiency requires adequate environment and little practice"); (3) Evolution explains individual differences (e.g., "he evolved to be smart") — confusing phylogenetic history with ontogenetic development. Concrete wrong answer: "A baby walking at 10 months instead of 12 months shows faster maturation" — actually shows individual variation in de
c12_ps_cbse_06_005	Students often believe that specialised agencies like WHO or UNICEF have enforcement power over sovereign states (e.g., "WHO can force a country to lockdown" or "UNICEF can prosecute child labour violators"). In reality, these agencies operate through technical cooperation, norms/standards, advocacy, and resource mobilisation — they have NO legislative, judicial, or coercive authority. For example, during COVID-19, WHO issued guidelines and declared a PHEIC, but compliance was voluntary. Confusing "norm-setting" with "enforcement" leads to overestimating UN power in board answers and competitive exams.
c11_psy_cbse_03_002	Students equate Life-Span Perspective with "development continues throughout life" (simple continuity) and miss its five other defining features. They treat LSP as merely extending the developmental timeline past adolescence, ignoring that multi-directionality means old age involves simultaneous wisdom gains and processing-speed losses; plasticity means modifiability within biological constraints, not unlimited potential; historical embeddedness means a 20-year-old in 1947 India had fundamentally different developmental affordances than a 20-year-old today; and multidisciplinarity means no single discipline (psychology alone) can fully explain development. Concrete wrong answer: "LSP means we keep developing until we die" — this reduces a 7-assumption paradigm to a single temporal claim.
c12_ps_cbse_06_006	Students think UN peacekeepers are a standing UN army that the Secretary-General can deploy anywhere. In reality, the UN has NO standing force. Every soldier and police officer is contributed by member states (Troop Contributing Countries - TCCs) who retain national command authority, negotiate caveats (e.g., 'no night patrols'), and can withdraw unilaterally. The Secretariat only manages logistics and strategy. This misconception leads to blaming 'the UN' for failures that are actually member state decisions.
c11_psy_cbse_03_003	Students believe "embryo" and "foetus" are just size differences, not qualitatively distinct developmental phases. They also think teratogens cause the same damage regardless of timing (e.g., "alcohol always causes FAS facial features"). Concrete example: A student answers "Thalidomide causes limb defects at any pregnancy stage" — wrong because thalidomide only causes phocomelia if taken days 20-36 post-conception (limb bud critical period).
c12_ps_cbse_06_007	Students often think the IMF and World Bank are "UN agencies" in the same way as WHO or UNESCO — subject to General Assembly control. In reality, they are specialised agencies with autonomous governance, separate funding, and weighted voting where the UN's "one state one vote" principle does NOT apply. Another error: confusing IMF's Structural Adjustment Programmes (SAPs) with World Bank's Structural Adjustment Loans (SALs) — both imposed conditionality but IMF's were macroeconomic (fiscal/monetary) while Bank's were sectoral (agriculture, trade liberalisation). This distinction is critical for board questions on "conditionality".
c11_psy_cbse_03_004	Students often think that **reflexes disappear because the baby “learns” not to do them** (i.e., voluntary suppression through practice). In reality, reflexes are **inhibited by maturing cortical circuits**; they fade on a genetically programmed timetable even without practice. For example, the Moro reflex vanishes around 6–7 months whether or not the baby is frequently startled — it is not “unlearned.” This misconception leads to wrong predictions: a student might say “if we prevent the Moro reflex from being elicited, it will persist longer,” whereas the correct view is that cortical maturation proceeds on its own schedule.
c12_ps_cbse_06_008	Students often think **the WTO is a 'world government' that makes laws for all countries**. In reality, the WTO is a **member-driven organisation** where decisions are taken by consensus — no member is bound by a rule it did not agree to. For example, the Doha Round stalled precisely because developing countries (including India) used their consensus power to block agreements they saw as harmful. The WTO Secretariat has no legislative power; it only provides technical support. This misconception leads to blaming the WTO for outcomes that are actually the result of negotiated compromises among sovereign states.
c11_psy_cbse_03_005	Students conflate **stage names** with **age norms**, treating them as fixed biological milestones (e.g., "At 7 years, a child *becomes* concrete operational"). They then misdiagnose a 7-year-old who fails conservation as "delayed" rather than recognising **horizontal décalage**—the same child may conserve number but not weight, or conserve liquid but not volume. This error stems from reading the *age ranges in Table 3.2* as deterministic thresholds instead of *approximate central tendencies* around which individual and cultural variation operates. For example, a student writes: "A 10-year-old who cannot solve the pendulum task has not reached formal operations"—ignoring that formal operations are *domain-specific* and the pendulum task requires **control-of-variables schema** that may not
c12_ps_cbse_06_009	Students often confuse the ICJ (UN's principal judicial organ, inter-state disputes only) with the International Criminal Court (ICC) (prosecutes individuals for genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity). They also believe ICJ jurisdiction is compulsory for all UN members — it is not; consent is required. Another error: thinking advisory opinions are legally binding — they are not, though they carry great legal weight.
c11_psy_cbse_03_006	**Students treat the eight stages as independent "boxes" to memorize, ignoring the epigenetic principle.** They write: "Stage 5 is Identity vs. Role Confusion. Virtue: Fidelity." But when asked "How does a toddler's shame (Stage 2) affect adolescent identity?" they cannot answer. The specific error: **They confuse the *crisis name* with the *developmental mechanism*.** For example, they think "Autonomy" means "independence" in the Western sense, so they mark "Indian toddlers don't show autonomy" as true. Actually, autonomy in Erikson means **voluntary control of behavior** (choosing to hold a spoon vs. being fed), which is universal. The cultural variation is in *how much choice is permitted*, not the existence of the crisis.
c12_ps_cbse_06_010	Students often think India's UNSC bid is 'blocked only by China' — writing 'China uses veto to stop India' in board answers. This is factually wrong and conceptually shallow. Reality: (1) UNSC expansion requires UNGA 2/3 majority + P5 ratification — China is one of five P5, but US, UK, France, Russia also must ratify; (2) 'Uniting for Consensus' (40+ nations including Italy, Pakistan) blocks consensus in IGN — China leverages this but didn't create it; (3) US supports India 'in principle' but opposes veto for new members — so even without China, P5 consensus fails. Students must distinguish: procedural block (IGN consensus) vs. ratification block (P5). Board marking scheme awards marks for identifying UfC as the primary procedural obstacle, not China alone.
c11_psy_cbse_03_007	Students believe moral *development* means making "better" decisions (e.g., "stealing is wrong" → "stealing is sometimes right"). They confuse *stage* with *verdict*. For example, a student classifies "Heinz shouldn't steal because it's illegal" as Stage 4, but "Heinz should steal because his wife will die" as Stage 6—thinking the pro-stealing answer is "higher." In reality, both could be Stage 1 if reasoning is "stealing gets you in trouble" vs. "I'd want someone to save me." The stage is determined *only* by the *justification structure*, not the behavioural choice.
c12_ps_cbse_07_001	Students often think "internal threat" in traditional security means any serious domestic problem — poverty, corruption, communal riots, or protests. In reality, traditional security only recognizes internal threats that involve **organized armed violence directly challenging the state's monopoly on legitimate force and territorial integrity** (e.g., insurgency, separatist rebellion, civil war). For example, students may correctly identify the Naxalite movement as a traditional internal threat but incorrectly label the 2020-21 farmer protests or the 1975 Emergency as traditional internal security threats. The former was non-violent democratic dissent; the latter was a constitutional crisis, not an armed challenge to state sovereignty.
c11_psy_cbse_03_008	Students often believe that "telegraphic speech" means the child speaks in short, incomplete sentences because of low intelligence or lack of exposure. In reality, telegraphic speech is a universal, biologically timed stage where children systematically omit function words (articles, auxiliaries, inflections) while retaining content words, demonstrating they have extracted the core syntactic skeleton of their language. For example, a child saying "Mommy go store" is not "being lazy" but correctly applying English SVO word order and dropping only the auxiliary "is" and article "the" — a pattern seen in all typically developing English learners regardless of IQ or input quantity.
c12_ps_cbse_07_002	Students often believe "Mutually Assured Destruction" means both sides are literally assured of total destruction in every scenario, and therefore MAD guarantees peace. In reality, MAD is a condition of strategic stability at the *strategic nuclear level* — it does not prevent conventional wars (Kargil, 1999), crises (Cuban Missile Crisis, 1962), or accidental escalation. Moreover, MAD assumes rational actors, perfect information, and survivable arsenals — conditions that may not hold in a crisis with short warning times (India-Pakistan) or with non-state actors who cannot be deterred by threats of retaliation. The misconception leads students to write "MAD prevented war" as a blanket statement in board exams, ignoring the stability-instability paradox and near-misses.
c11_psy_cbse_03_009	Students frequently believe that gender identity is fixed at birth and entirely determined by biology ("born this way"), leading them to view gender socialisation as merely "revealing" innate traits rather than actively constructing them. For example, a student might argue: "Boys naturally prefer trucks because of prenatal testosterone, so giving them trucks isn't socialisation – it's just nature." This misconception arises from: (1) oversimplified media reporting on hormone studies; (2) confusion between sex differences (average group differences) and gender identity (individual sense of self); (3) lack of exposure to evidence that gender-typed toy preferences emerge *after* gender labelling (around age 2-3), not before; (4) cultural essentialism in Indian discourse ("boys will be boys").
c12_ps_cbse_07_003	Students often think 'non-traditional security' is just a new label for 'non-military problems' and that the state's military can still handle them (e.g., "army built hospitals during COVID, so military handles health security"). This confuses 'capacity' with 'paradigm'. The military was a last-resort logistics provider; the security logic — prevention, surveillance, international health regulations, equity in vaccine access — is fundamentally civilian, cooperative, and people-centric. Another error: equating non-traditional security only with terrorism (which is often treated as traditional/non-traditional hybrid). Terrorism is covered separately in c12_ps_cbse_07_004; non-traditional threats are broader and structural.
c11_psy_cbse_03_010	Students believe "adolescent egocentrism" means adolescents are selfish or narcissistic. In reality, Elkind's imaginary audience and personal fable are COGNITIVE LIMITATIONS of early formal operations: the adolescent's newfound ability to think about others' thoughts leads to OVER-estimating how much others think about them. For example, a student who thinks "Everyone noticed my wrong answer in class" is not being self-centered—they are unable to differentiate their own intense self-focus from others' actual attention. This misconception causes teachers/parents to moralise ("stop being so self-absorbed") instead of scaffolding perspective-taking.
c12_ps_cbse_07_004	Students often conflate 'terrorism' with 'insurgency' or 'freedom struggle', arguing that "one man's terrorist is another man's freedom fighter." This relativism ignores the NCERT's clear criterion: terrorism deliberately targets civilians; insurgency targets state security forces to control territory. For example, Kashmiri militants attacking army convoys is insurgency/guerrilla warfare; the same group bombing a civilian market in Delhi is terrorism. The strategic logic differs: insurgency seeks territorial control; terrorism seeks psychological coercion. This misconception leads to flawed policy analysis — e.g., suggesting political autonomy solves terrorism when it only addresses insurgency grievances.
c11_psy_cbse_03_011	Students believe that "ageing = uniform decline for everyone" and that developmental stages in adulthood are rigidly age-locked (e.g., "retirement at 60 means old age starts"). They confuse normative ageing (universal, gradual changes like presbyopia, slower processing) with pathological ageing (dementia, severe disability), and assume Erikson's stages imply everyone resolves crises at the same age. For example, a student might write: "A 65-year-old cannot learn new skills because brain plasticity ends at 25," ignoring NCERT's explicit statement that "development is highly plastic... skills and abilities can be improved throughout the life-span" and the example of active 70+ year-olds in politics, literature, and science.
c12_ps_cbse_07_005	Students often equate human security exclusively with "soft" issues like humanitarian aid or development, ignoring the "freedom from fear" pillar that includes protection from violence, genocide, human rights abuses, and conflict. This leads to answers that treat human security as the opposite of military security, rather than a broader framework that includes protection from physical violence alongside freedom from want.
c11_psy_cbse_04_001	Students believe sensation and perception occur in strict temporal sequence — first all sensation finishes, then perception begins — like two separate assembly-line stages. In reality, they are simultaneous and reciprocal: top-down perceptual hypotheses (e.g., "this is a face") modulate sensory gain (enhancing eye-region processing) within 80-100 ms, before conscious awareness. This error arises because textbook diagrams show linear arrows (stimulus → receptor → brain → perception) and students over-literalise the diagram.
c12_ps_cbse_07_006	Students often think "environmental security = protecting nature" or "climate change causes wars directly." The first confuses *conservation* (intrinsic value of nature) with *security* (human/state survival). The second ignores the *mediating role of politics*: the 2011 East Africa drought caused famine in Somalia (weak state, conflict) but not in Kenya (stronger institutions). Environmental stress becomes a security threat only when it interacts with governance failure, inequality, and identity politics. Writing "climate change causes conflict" in board exams loses marks for oversimplification; the correct formulation is "climate change exacerbates drivers of conflict."
c11_psy_cbse_04_002	Students treat absolute and difference thresholds as fixed, universal constants (like "the absolute threshold for vision is 1 photon") rather than probabilistic, context-dependent estimates. They answer "AL is the minimum stimulus you can detect" and miss the 50% criterion, leading to errors in board questions asking "Why is AL determined over multiple trials?" or "Why does AL vary for the same person on different days?" The root error: confusing a statistical operating characteristic with a physiological hard limit.
c12_ps_cbse_07_007	Students often believe that health pandemics, poverty, and food security are merely 'development issues' or 'humanitarian concerns', not 'real security threats' because they lack a identifiable enemy or military dimension. They write answers like 'these are problems for the Health Ministry or Agriculture Ministry, not the Defence Ministry', failing to grasp that the human security framework deliberately expands the security agenda to include threats that kill more people than wars — and that the state's legitimacy now depends on managing them.
c11_psy_cbse_04_003	Students often believe the lens is the primary refractive structure of the eye because cameras use lenses for focusing. In reality, the cornea provides ~70% of total refractive power (due to air-cornea interface) while the lens provides fine-tuning via accommodation. This misconception leads to errors in explaining why corneal damage causes severe refractive errors, why contact lenses work on the corneal surface, and why lens removal (cataract surgery) still permits functional vision with correction.
c12_ps_cbse_07_008	Students often believe cooperative security is synonymous with **collective security** (e.g., "UN sends troops automatically") or that it only applies to military alliances like NATO. In reality, cooperative security is a **voluntary, multi-tool strategy** covering arms control (NPT, CTBT), confidence-building (hotlines, data exchanges), economic sanctions regimes, and non-military threats (health, climate). They also think it requires **world government** — but it operates through **intergovernmental institutions** where states retain veto power (e.g., UNSC P5). This leads to wrong answers like "cooperative security failed in Syria because UN didn't intervene" — confusing it with collective security enforcement.
c11_psy_cbse_04_004	Students believe the **cochlea is a simple microphone** that converts sound waves into neural signals "all at once" — like a light sensor converting photons to current. They think: "Sound vibrates the eardrum → bones push fluid → hair cells fire → brain hears." This misses three critical nonlinearities: (1) **Impedance matching** (middle ear transformer), (2) **Frequency-place mapping** (traveling wave on basilar membrane), (3) **Active amplification** by outer hair cells (OHCs) that sharpens tuning and provides compressive nonlinearity. For example, when asked "Why does a 1000 Hz tone at 20 dB sound louder than a 100 Hz tone at 20 dB?", the student answers "Because 1000 Hz has higher frequency" — confusing physical frequency with perceptual loudness, and ignoring the ear's frequency-depen
c12_ps_cbse_07_009	Students often think "India's security policy is purely reactive/military" — they cite surgical strikes but miss the simultaneous diplomatic track (Composite Dialogue 2004-2008, Kartarpur Corridor 2019), economic integration attempts (SAFTA, MFN status), and the political-socioeconomic architecture for internal threats (Sixth Schedule, PESA, surrender-rehabilitation policies). They also conflate "China threat" as only military, ignoring the economic leverage (trade deficit $83B FY23), technology competition (5G, semiconductors), and multilateral dimensions (BRI, String of Pearls, Quad).
c11_psy_cbse_04_005	Students believe taste buds are only on the tongue and that each taste maps to a specific tongue region (tongue map myth). They also think kinesthetic and vestibular senses are the same "balance sense." In reality: taste buds exist on soft palate, epiglottis, pharynx, and upper oesophagus; all taste qualities are detected across all tongue regions (though thresholds vary); kinesthetic sense informs limb position and movement (proprioception) while vestibular sense detects head rotation/linear acceleration for balance and gaze stability. The tongue map originated from a 1901 misinterpretation of Hänig's data — modern electrophysiology shows broad tuning across the tongue. Students confuse these because textbooks often oversimplify and diagrams show segregated zones.
c12_ps_cbse_07_010	Students often think 'balancing' means a 50-50 split of budget or attention between defence and welfare. In reality, the balance is qualitative: state security must be *subordinated* to human security in a democracy — the military serves the people, not vice versa. For example, the Supreme Court in Naga People's Movement (1998) upheld AFSPA but mandated strict guidelines (Do's and Don'ts) precisely to prevent state security operations from becoming the primary source of human insecurity. The error is treating them as two equal pillars rather than a hierarchy of ends and means.
c11_psy_cbse_04_006	Students believe "divided attention" means truly parallel processing of two complex tasks (e.g., "I can study and watch TV effectively"). They confuse the subjective feeling of switching with actual simultaneous processing. The NCERT explicitly states divided attention works ONLY for highly practiced/automatic tasks (Box 4.1). Students also think selective attention is a voluntary choice ("I choose to ignore noise"), missing the involuntary capture by intense/novel stimuli (external factors) and the structural bottleneck (filter theories). They conflate "span of attention" (immediate perceptual span, 7±2 items) with "sustained attention duration" (hours of vigilance).
c12_ps_cbse_08_001	Students believe Partition was inevitable because 'Hindus and Muslims always hated each other' — a primordialist view. The NCERT shows Partition resulted from specific 1940s political choices: Congress rejection of compulsory grouping (1946), League's Direct Action Day (1946), British haste to exit (Mountbatten Plan), and the Radcliffe Award's district-level mechanical application. The 'ancient hatreds' narrative ignores the 1916 Lucknow Pact, 1920s Khilafat-Non-Cooperation unity, and the 1946 Cabinet Mission's near-success — evidence that communalism was politically constructed, not historically predetermined.
c11_psy_cbse_04_007	Students often believe 'internal factors' mean only conscious, voluntary goals (e.g., 'I decide to pay attention to the teacher'). They miss that internal factors include automatic motivational states (hunger, thirst) and implicit preparatory sets (schemas) that operate without awareness. For example, a student says 'I noticed the canteen smell because I wanted to' — confusing post-hoc rationalisation with the automatic threshold-lowering effect of hunger. This error stems from equating 'internal' with 'intentional', ignoring the textbook's distinction between motivational factors (biological needs) and cognitive factors (interest, attitude, preparatory set) where only the latter involve conscious disposition.
c12_ps_cbse_08_002	Students often believe Sardar Patel used *only* force or coercion to integrate princely states, citing Hyderabad and Junagadh as proof. In reality, over 560 states (99%) acceded peacefully via the Instrument of Accession before 15 August 1947 through diplomatic negotiation led by V.P. Menon and Patel. The misconception arises from textbook emphasis on the *exceptional* cases (Hyderabad, Junagadh, Kashmir) which required force, while the *norm* was a negotiated surrender of paramountcy powers. For example, the Maharaja of Mysore, the Nizam of Travancore (after initial hesitation), and the rulers of Baroda, Gwalior, and Bikaner signed IoAs voluntarily, motivated by popular pressure, economic interdependence, and Patel's assurance of privy purses and internal autonomy.
c11_psy_cbse_04_008	Students often believe that **each Gestalt principle operates in isolation and that a single principle "explains" a given percept**. In reality, every natural scene contains simultaneous cues for proximity, similarity, continuity, closure, etc., and the final percept is the outcome of a **parallel, competitive integration** where cues are weighted by their salience. For example, in a row of alternating red circles and blue squares spaced equally, a student may say "Proximity makes them one row" ignoring that Similarity would predict two colour groups or two shape groups. The error stems from textbook figures that isolate one principle at a time, leading students to treat principles as mutually exclusive rules rather than as weighted votes in a perceptual election.
c12_ps_cbse_08_003	**Misconception**: "Junagadh was integrated by force like Hyderabad." **Reality**: Junagadh's integration was **peaceful and democratic**. The Nawab acceded to Pakistan (Aug 1947), but the **Hindu-majority population revolted**, the Nawab fled, and a **provisional government (Aarzi Hukumat)** took over with India's support. India **blockaded** Junagadh but **did not send troops**; instead, it **insisted on a plebiscite** (Feb 1948), which returned **99% in favour of India**. The misconception arises from conflating the **two most famous "difficult" accessions** and assuming "use of force" applies to both. Students must distinguish: **Hyderabad = military action after failed diplomacy + internal tyranny; Junagadh = plebiscite after ruler's flight + popular revolt**.
c11_psy_cbse_04_009	Students often believe perceptual constancy means the retinal image *does not change* — they think "constancy" applies to the sensory input rather than the percept. For example, when asked "What happens to the retinal image of a car as it drives toward you?", many answer "It stays the same size because of size constancy." This error arises because textbook definitions emphasize perceptual stability ("object appears same size") without explicitly contrasting it with the *necessary* retinal change. The misconception is reinforced when students confuse the *outcome* (stable percept) with the *input* (changing retinal image), missing the entire point that constancy is an active compensatory process.
c12_ps_cbse_08_004	Students often believe Article 370 gave J&K a "separate constitution" and "dual citizenship" in the same way a federal unit has in a classic federation (like US states). In reality, J&K's Constitution (1957) was *subordinate* to the Indian Constitution — it could not contradict central laws on Union/Concurrent lists, and "dual citizenship" meant only state subject rights (property, employment) under Article 35A, not a separate national citizenship. This misconception leads to overestimating J&K's sovereignty and underestimating the central government's existing powers before 2019.
c11_psy_cbse_04_010	Students often believe that "illusions prove perception is unreliable" or "illusions are errors the brain should avoid." This is wrong because illusions demonstrate the brain's *successful* use of probabilistic inference: in natural 3D environments, the Muller-Lyer configuration *would* indicate different distances (outside vs. inside corner), so the size-distance scaling computation is ecologically valid. The illusion only occurs in the artificial 2D lab setting where the depth cue is decoupled from actual distance. Students also confuse "universal illusion" (same direction for all humans) with "universal magnitude" (same strength for all) — susceptibility varies continuously due to individual differences in perceptual learning, not a binary present/absent trait.
c12_ps_cbse_08_005	Students often believe the Constituent Assembly debates were merely about 'borrowing' features from other constitutions (e.g., UK, USA, Ireland). In reality, the most consequential debates — on the strength of the Centre, the language formula, the inclusion of Directive Principles as non-justiciable goals, and the safeguards for minorities — were driven by India's immediate existential challenges (Partition, princely states, diversity) and produced original constitutional innovations not found in any borrowed model.
c11_psy_cbse_04_011	Students often think “cultural influence on perception” means people from different cultures *see different physical realities* (e.g., “Africans literally see the vertical line as longer”). The correct understanding is that the *interpretive habit* differs: the same retinal image triggers a different perceptual inference because the cultural environment has calibrated the perceptual system’s priors. For example, a Westerner and a Zulu both receive the same Müller-Lyer figure on their retina, but the Westerner’s visual system, tuned to right-angled corners, automatically applies a depth-constancy scaling that makes the arrow-head line look shorter. This is not a difference in sensation but in unconscious inference.
c12_ps_cbse_08_006	**Misconception:** "Nehru's secularism meant the state stays completely out of religion (Western 'wall of separation')." **Reality:** Nehru supported the *Indian model* — **principled distance** (Rajeev Bhargava): state *intervenes* to reform harmful practices (Hindu Code Bills 1955–56 abolishing polygamy, enabling divorce, giving daughters inheritance rights) while funding minority institutions (Article 30). Students confuse Nehru with the French *laïcité* model; they miss that Nehru *used state power* to modernise Hindu personal law but *not* Muslim personal law — a selective reform that later fueled the Uniform Civil Code debate (Shah Bano, 1985).
c11_psy_cbse_05_001	Students equate "relatively permanent" with "permanent forever" and argue that forgetting disproves learning. They also confuse *performance* (observable behaviour at a moment) with *learning* (the inferred underlying change). For example, a student who crams for an exam, performs well, then forgets everything a week later claims "no learning occurred." This misreads NCERT: learning *did* occur (relatively permanent change at that time), but extinction/forgetting happened later. The error stems from treating learning as a static state rather than a process with a trajectory.
c12_ps_cbse_08_007	Students often believe the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 created *all* current Indian states on linguistic lines. In reality, the 1956 Act created 14 states and 6 UTs; many present states (Maharashtra, Gujarat, Punjab, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand, Jharkhand, Telangana, and all Northeastern states except Assam) were formed *later* through separate Acts, often on bases *beyond* language (culture, ecology, development). This misconception leads to wrong answers in board questions asking "Which state was NOT formed in 1956?" or "Was language the only basis?"
c11_psy_cbse_05_002	Students believe the neutral stimulus **becomes** the unconditioned stimulus after conditioning (e.g., "the bell turns into food for the dog"). They think the CS physically transforms or that the dog "expects" food cognitively. In reality, the bell remains a bell—it gains **signal value** through temporal contiguity and contingency, triggering a preparatory physiological response (salivation) that anticipates the US. The dog does not salivate "because it knows food is coming"; it salivates because the neural pathway from auditory cortex to salivary nuclei has been strengthened by repeated CS–US pairing.
c12_ps_cbse_08_008	Students often think the Planning Commission was a constitutional body like the Election Commission or Finance Commission. In reality, it was created by an executive resolution (Cabinet decision) in 1950, had no statutory backing, and its Chairperson (PM) and Deputy Chairperson were political appointees. This matters because it meant the Commission's authority derived from political consensus, not constitutional mandate — making it easier to replace with NITI Aayog in 2015 without a constitutional amendment.
c11_psy_cbse_05_003	Students often believe that extinction means the conditioned response is "unlearned" or permanently erased, so they are surprised by spontaneous recovery. They also think generalisation is a sign of poor discrimination or stupidity, rather than an adaptive feature where organisms respond to stimuli that resemble a biologically significant cue. For example, a student might write: "After extinction, the dog no longer associates the bell with food, so spontaneous recovery shouldn't happen." This error arises because they confuse the behavioural output (performance) with the underlying associative strength, ignoring that extinction creates a new inhibitory memory that coexists with the original excitatory memory.
c12_ps_cbse_08_009	Students often believe the first elections were a smooth, uncontested Congress victory because of Nehru's popularity, overlooking the massive logistical hurdles (173 million voters, 224,000 polling booths, 2 million ballot boxes), the vibrant multi-party opposition, and the fact that the Election Commission had to innovate procedures (symbols, indelible ink, simultaneous elections) from scratch. They also confuse the 1951-52 voting age (21) with the current age (18), and assume universal franchise was uncontroversial — ignoring debates in the Constituent Assembly about literacy qualifications.
c11_psy_cbse_05_004	Students consistently equate "negative reinforcement" with "punishment" because the word "negative" carries a colloquial meaning of "bad" or "aversive." They therefore classify taking aspirin to remove a headache as punishment (since headache is unpleasant) rather than negative reinforcement (removal of headache strengthens aspirin-taking). This error persists even after definitions are memorised because the sign of the contingency (removal vs. presentation) and the direction of behaviour change (increase vs. decrease) are not visually contrasted in typical textbook tables.
c12_ps_cbse_08_010	Students often believe "rehabilitation was just about giving land to refugees" and miss the constitutional crisis: the same state that allotted Muslim homes to Hindu/Sikh refugees had to simultaneously protect Muslim citizens' property in India (e.g., in Delhi, UP) to uphold Articles 14, 15, 25. They also conflate "refugees" with "minorities" — Punjabi Hindu/Sikh refugees became a majority in East Punjab, while Muslims in India remained a vulnerable minority. This confusion leads to wrong answers like "the state favored Hindus" instead of "the state used compensatory justice for displaced persons while struggling to protect a minority under majoritarian pressure."
c11_psy_cbse_05_005	Students equate **negative reinforcement** with **punishment** because both involve "unpleasant" stimuli. They write: "Negative reinforcement is when you get scolded so you stop doing it." This is wrong: negative reinforcement **increases** a behaviour (escape/avoidance) by **removing** an aversive stimulus (e.g., putting on a seatbelt stops the annoying beep). Punishment **decreases** a behaviour by **adding** an aversive (scolding) or **removing** a pleasant stimulus (phone confiscated). The error arises from everyday language where "negative" = "bad", but in operant terminology "negative" = **subtraction/removal**.
c12_ps_cbse_09_001	Students often believe Congress dominance meant India was a de facto one-party state like China or USSR, or that opposition parties were banned/suppressed. The exact error: confusing 'one-party dominance' (a single party wins repeatedly in free, fair, multi-party elections) with 'one-party system' (constitutionally/legally only one party allowed). Evidence: In 1952, 53 parties and 1,874 independents contested; Communist Party won 16 seats; opposition leaders like Ambedkar and Shyama Prasad Mukherjee served in Nehru's first cabinet. The NCERT explicitly states: "Many parties contested elections in conditions of free and fair elections and yet the Congress managed to win election after election."
c11_psy_cbse_05_006	Students often believe observational learning is simply "copying" or "imitation" and therefore requires the observer to perform the behaviour immediately while watching. They miss that Bandura's theory posits learning (acquisition) as a covert cognitive process — attention, retention, and symbolic coding — that can occur without any overt behaviour, and that performance depends on a separate motivational process (vicarious reinforcement/punishment). For example, a student might say "The child didn't learn because they didn't do it right away," confusing performance with learning.
c12_ps_cbse_09_002	Students often think "Congress dominance = absence of real democracy" or "Congress won because opposition parties were banned." In reality, multiple parties (CPI, Socialists, Jana Sangh, etc.) contested freely, won seats, and criticized the government; Congress dominance came from its ability to aggregate votes across a fragmented opposition under FPTP, not from suppressing rivals. Another error: "Factions weakened Congress." Actually, factions acted as safety valves that kept ambitious leaders inside the party, preventing splits that could have created stronger opposition.
c11_psy_cbse_05_007	Students believe insight learning is simply "fast learning" or "learning without practice" — they equate the *suddenness* of the solution with *ease* of acquisition. For example, when asked "How many trials did Sultan need?", they answer "One!" ignoring the 30-minute incubation period where Sultan manipulated boxes, stared at the banana, and appeared inactive. This misconception arises because textbooks emphasize the "aha!" moment while underplaying the preparatory struggle. Students then incorrectly predict that insight learning should work for *any* problem instantly, failing to recognize that preparation (gathering relevant information) and incubation (unconscious processing) are necessary preconditions — you cannot have an insight about calculus if you don't know algebra.
c12_ps_cbse_09_003	Students believe Congress won 1952 *only* because of Nehru's charisma or freedom struggle legacy, ignoring the structural amplification of FPTP: Congress's 45% vote became 74% seats *because* opposition votes were split among 4+ parties per constituency on average. They also confuse "one-party dominance" (democratic, competitive elections with one consistent winner) with "one-party system" (legal ban on opposition, e.g., China). The NCERT explicitly contrasts these on p. 35-36.
c11_psy_cbse_05_008	Students often confuse *latent learning* with *insight learning*, thinking both involve "sudden understanding." They write: "The rats suddenly realised the maze layout on Day 11." This is wrong because latent learning is *gradual and incidental* during exploration (Days 1–10); only the *performance* is sudden. The error stems from equating "sudden performance change" with "sudden learning." Another error: "Latent learning means learning without any reinforcement ever." This ignores that reinforcement is essential to *elicit* the behaviour — Tolman's Group 2 needed food on Day 11 to show what they knew.
c12_ps_cbse_09_004	Students often believe the Socialist Party was a single, unified party that simply "lost elections" and disappeared. In reality, it was a sequence of distinct parties (Socialist Party → KMPP → PSP → SSP → PSP again → Samyukta Socialist Party) with different leaderships, ideologies, and electoral strategies. The "decline" is actually a history of repeated fragmentation and failed reunifications, not a linear fade-out. Another misconception: that the 1955 Avadi resolution caused an immediate merger — in fact, the Socialist Party continued for over a decade after 1955, splitting *because* of the debate over how to respond to Avadi.
c11_psy_cbse_05_009	Students believe the three phases are strictly time-based (e.g., "cognitive phase lasts 2 weeks") and that *automaticity means the skill no longer requires any brain involvement*. They also think "practice makes perfect" implies linear improvement, missing that plateaus are *necessary transitions* where the brain reorganises control from conscious to subcortical structures. Example wrong answer: "After 20 hours of driving practice, I'll be in autonomous phase" — ignoring that phase transition depends on *quality of processing* (error analysis, variability), not just hours.
c12_ps_cbse_09_005	Students often believe the CPI was always a parliamentary party from its inception, overlooking its 1948-51 Telangana armed uprising and the 1951 strategic pivot. They also conflate CPI and CPI(M), assuming the 1964 split was merely personal rather than a deep ideological rupture over the Sino-Soviet split and the path to revolution (peaceful vs. armed). Another error is thinking the 1957 Kerala government was dismissed for corruption — it was dismissed after a Congress-led "liberation struggle" against its land reforms.
c11_psy_cbse_05_010	Students believe "learning disabilities mean the child is 'slow' or has low intelligence." This error arises because the term "disability" triggers a global deficit schema. In reality, NCERT defines learning disabilities as specific deficits in reading/writing/math *despite* average-to-superior intelligence, adequate sensory-motor function, and opportunity. For example, a child with dyslexia may have a 120 IQ but cannot distinguish 'b' from 'd' due to phonological processing deficits, not low intelligence. The misconception persists because classroom observations often confound effort, attention, and specific skill deficits.
c12_ps_cbse_09_006	**Misconception**: "The Bharatiya Jana Sangh was the same as the BJP and was a major challenger to Congress in the 1950s." **Reality**: The **BJS (1951–1977)** won only **3 seats (1952) and 4 seats (1957)** — a **marginal force**. The **BJP was formed in 1980** after the Janata Party collapsed. The BJS’s **ideological core (Hindutva, RSS cadre)** continued, but its **electoral trajectory, leadership, and coalition strategies** changed dramatically. Students who conflate the two cannot explain why the BJP’s breakthrough came **three decades later** (post-1984, Ram Mandir movement, Mandal politics).
c11_psy_cbse_06_001	Students often believe that any repetition (maintenance rehearsal) automatically transfers information into long-term memory. They equate “studying” with reading notes aloud repeatedly, not realizing that without semantic analysis (elaborative rehearsal) the information merely cycles in short-term memory and decays once repetition stops. For example, a student may recite a definition 20 times, feel confident, yet blank on the exam because the material never reached LTM.
c12_ps_cbse_09_007	**Misconception:** "The Swatantra Party was just a party of **feudal landlords and princes** defending their privileges." **Reality:** While it *drew support* from landed elites (especially after Congress land reforms), its **ideology** was articulated by modern liberals (Masani — economist, Dandekar — statistician, Rajaji — constitutionalist) using *universal* classical liberal arguments (Hayek, Friedman), not feudal rhetoric. They opposed land ceilings *on principle* (property rights), not just self-interest. Students who reduce it to "feudal party" miss the **intellectual history** of Indian liberalism and cannot explain why urban professionals and traders also joined.
c11_psy_cbse_06_002	Students believe sensory memory is "where memories start" — i.e., that iconic/echoic memory is the *first step of memorisation*. They think: "I see something → it goes into iconic memory → if I pay attention, it becomes a memory." This is wrong because sensory memory is a *perceptual buffer*, not a memory store in the meaningful sense. It holds raw, unprocessed sensory data (like a camera sensor), not encoded information. The error arises from the word "memory" in the term and from textbook diagrams showing it as "Stage 1" in a linear flow. Concrete wrong answer: "Iconic memory is where visual memories are first stored before moving to STM."
c12_ps_cbse_09_008	Students believe opposition parties in the 1950s were 'irrelevant' because they won few seats, and that Congress dominance meant 'no real democracy.' They confuse electoral dominance with democratic deficit, ignoring that: (a) multiple parties contested freely, (b) opposition criticism shaped policy (e.g., CPI's Kerala victory forced land reform debates), (c) the 'Congress system' internalised competition, and (d) the 1957 Kerala Communist government proved opposition could win state power. This misconception costs marks in board questions asking 'Was India a democracy in the 1950s?' and in CUET/JEE-style analytical questions on party systems.
c11_psy_cbse_06_003	Students often believe that **Short-Term Memory and Working Memory are synonymous terms for the same "short-duration memory store."** They incorrectly treat the Phonological Loop as *the* STM, ignoring the Central Executive and Visuospatial Sketchpad. This leads to errors like: (1) Attributing all short-term holding to "STM capacity 7±2" without distinguishing verbal vs. visual domains; (2) Assuming maintenance rehearsal is the *only* control process in STM, overlooking elaborative rehearsal's role in LTM transfer; (3) Interpreting the KF case study as "proof STM is not needed for LTM" rather than "verbal STM (Phonological Loop) is not the *only* route to LTM." c12_ps_cbse_09_009	Students often think the "Syndicate" was a formal constitutional body within the Congress (like the CWC) or that it was synonymous with the "High Command." In reality, the Syndicate was an *informal, unelected clique* of 5-6 regional bosses who *captured* the formal organs (CWC, Parliamentary Board) through mutual patronage. They were not "the High Command" — the High Command (Nehru/Indira) was the parliamentary leadership; the Syndicate was the *organizational* leadership that often *defied* the High Command. Another error: assuming the Syndicate represented "internal democracy" because it included regional leaders. c11_psy_cbse_06_004	**Misconception:** "Declarative memory is 'knowing that' and procedural memory is 'knowing how'—so if I can explain *how* to do something, it's declarative." **Why it's wrong:** This confuses *declarative knowledge about a procedure* (semantic memory) with *procedural memory itself*. A student can verbally describe the steps of a cricket cover drive (semantic/declarative) but completely lack the procedural memory to execute it. Procedural memory is defined by **non-verbalizability and automatic performance**, not by the content being a "procedure." The error arises because everyday language uses "know how" for both the *description* and the *skill*; psychology distinguishes the *representation format* (propositional vs. procedural).
c12_ps_cbse_09_010	Students often write: "Congress declined because Indira Gandhi became authoritarian and split the party in 1969." This reverses causality. The split was a *symptom* of deeper decay: the Congress system's inability to manage succession after Nehru (1964), the FPTP system's vulnerability to opposition vote consolidation (1967), and the rise of new social groups (middle peasants, backward castes) that the Syndicate-dominated organization could not accommodate. Indira's "authoritarianism" was her *response* to organizational paralysis — she used state power (PM's office) to capture the party because the party organization (Syndicate) blocked her. The misconception costs marks in board exams because it ignores structural factors (electoral system, social change, federal dynamics) that the NCERT
c11_psy_cbse_06_005	Students often believe "deeper processing = more time spent studying". They equate duration with depth, so they re-read notes for hours (maintenance rehearsal) thinking it is semantic encoding. In reality, 10 minutes of generating personal examples (elaborative) outperforms 60 minutes of passive re-reading because depth is defined by *meaning extraction and connection*, not clock time. This misconception arises from conflating effort (time) with cognitive operations (analysis of meaning).
c12_ps_cbse_10_001	**Misconception:** "The Planning Commission was a constitutional body like the Election Commission, and it had the power to implement plans directly." **Reality:** It was created by a **cabinet resolution** (executive order), not by the Constitution or Parliament. It had **zero implementation powers** — it only *formulated* plans and *allocated* plan outlays. Actual implementation was by **central ministries and state governments**. The Union Cabinet had to approve its recommendations. This confusion leads students to write in exams that "the Planning Commission built Bhakra Nangal Dam" — incorrect; the *state government* built it using *plan funds allocated by the Commission*.
c11_psy_cbse_06_006	**Misconception:** "Ebbinghaus's curve means *most* forgetting happens in the first 20 minutes, so if I survive the first hour, I'm safe." **Why it's wrong:** Students misread the curve's *steepest segment* (first hour) as the *only* significant forgetting window, ignoring that the **asymptotic tail still accounts for 20-30% additional loss over days** — and that **without spaced review, the curve resets with each new learning episode**. This error stems from treating the curve as a one-time event rather than a recurring pattern for *each* memory trace. **Concrete wrong answer:** "I'll just review once after 1 hour and I'll remember it forever." → This student will show catastrophic forgetting at the 1-week mark because they didn't schedule reviews at the *inflection points* of the curve (
c12_ps_cbse_10_002	Students often think the First Plan "neglected industry" or was "anti-industrial" because it focused on agriculture. In reality, the Plan explicitly stated that agricultural surplus and raw materials (cotton, jute, food for industrial workers) were *preconditions* for sustainable industrialisation. The misconception arises from reading the sectoral allocation table (agriculture ~15%, industry ~8%) without reading the Plan's own logic: industry cannot grow if workers starve and factories lack raw cotton. The Second Plan's industrial push *depended* on the First Plan's agrarian foundation — a sequential strategy, not a sectoral prejudice.
c11_psy_cbse_06_007	**Misconception**: "Proactive and retroactive interference are just 'forgetting because of other learning' — the direction (past→future vs future→past) doesn't matter for explaining real-life forgetting." **Why it's wrong**: Direction *determines the experimental design* (Table 6.1) and *real-world intervention*. Example: A student learns French (List A) then Spanish (List B). If they fail Spanish recall, **retroactive interference** (French→Spanish) implies *spacing French/Spanish study* helps. If they fail French recall, **proactive interference** (French→Spanish) implies *learning Spanish first* or *overlearning French* helps. Confusing direction leads to *opposite study advice*. c12_ps_cbse_10_003	Students often believe the Mahalanobis model was a direct copy of the Soviet Feldman model. In reality, Mahalanobis independently developed a similar two-sector closed-economy model using Indian input-output data and statistical expertise; the Soviet influence was political (socialist pattern) not technical. Another error: thinking the Second Plan neglected agriculture entirely — it allocated ~20% to agriculture/irrigation, but the *growth* strategy hinged on industry.
c11_psy_cbse_06_008	**Misconception**: "Memory works like a video camera — it records events faithfully and replays them on demand. If you can't remember something, it's because the recording faded, not because the memory was *changed*." **Why it's wrong**: This reproductive model cannot explain Bartlett's systematic distortions (participants didn't just *lose* details — they *changed* them in predictable, schema-driven directions) or the misinformation effect (post-event information doesn't just *overwrite* memories — it *integrates* into the reconstructed memory, becoming indistinguishable from the original). The misconception arises because the *subjective experience* of remembering *feels* like playback — we experience memories as "vivid" and "accurate" — but this feeling is itself a reconstruction. c12_ps_cbse_10_004	Students think the agriculture-industry debate was simply "Nehru vs Gandhians" or "socialists vs capitalists." In reality, the *Congress party itself* contained both currents: the Avadi Resolution (1955) declared "socialist pattern of society" *before* the Second Plan, yet the First Plan (under Nehru) was agrarian. The debate cut across party lines—Charan Singh (Congress) later championed agriculture, while industrialists (Bombay Plan) *supported* state-led heavy industry. The misconception arises from reading later political alignments (1970s+) back into the 1950s.
c11_psy_cbse_06_009	Students believe that *any* mnemonic (e.g., a first-letter acronym) automatically improves memory for *any* material. They create "VIBGYOR-style" sentences for *conceptual* content (e.g., "Some People Cook Rice" for stages of photosynthesis) and wonder why they cannot *explain* the process in the exam. The error: confusing *serial recall cues* (first-letter) with *semantic understanding* (deep processing). First-letter techniques only cue the *labels* of steps, not their *mechanisms, order logic, or conditions*. The textbook explicitly warns: "Mnemonic strategies... are too simplistic and perhaps underestimate complexities of memory tasks" and recommends deep processing *alongside* mnemonics.
c12_ps_cbse_10_005	Students often think the Green Revolution was simply "new seeds" that spread naturally because they were better. In reality, it was a **state-engineered political project**: the Indian state chose specific seeds (dwarf wheat from CIMMYT, not indigenous varieties), built the irrigation and credit infrastructure only in chosen regions, guaranteed procurement prices only for wheat/rice, and subsidised inputs for adopting farmers. The "spread" was not market-driven — it was the result of deliberate resource allocation. For example, students write "farmers adopted HYV seeds because they gave higher yields" but miss that without assured irrigation, subsidised fertiliser, and guaranteed MSP procurement, the risk of HYV cultivation was prohibitive for most farmers. c11_psy_cbse_06_010	Students believe eyewitness memory works like a video camera — if you "saw it," the memory is stored intact and retrieval simply plays it back. They specifically think: (1) High confidence = high accuracy because "I know what I saw," (2) Cross-race effect is "racism" rather than perceptual expertise difference, (3) Leading questions only affect suggestible people, not "smart" witnesses. Example wrong answer: "The witness is 100% sure so it must be correct — why would they lie?" This ignores that confidence is malleable, memory is reconstructive, and witnesses genuinely believe distorted memories.
c12_ps_cbse_10_006	Students often think "mixed economy" means a 50-50 split between public and private sectors, or that the private sector was marginalized in the 1950s. In reality, the public sector dominated only 17 "Schedule A" industries (heavy/strategic), while the private sector flourished in consumer goods, textiles, jute, and light engineering — protected by high tariffs and licences. The private sector's share of *total industrial output* actually *rose* from 70% (1950) to 75% (1965) because the Plan expanded the *overall* industrial pie. The misconception stems from conflating "state planning" with "state ownership of everything."
c11_psy_cbse_07_001	Students equate "thinking" with *any* conscious mental activity — daydreaming, worrying, recalling a phone number, or perceiving a face. They write: "Thinking is when thoughts come to mind." This error arises because everyday language uses 'think' loosely ("I think it'll rain", "I can't think of her name"). In psychology, thinking is *not* passive occurrence of thoughts but *active, goal-directed manipulation of mental representations* (images/concepts). For example, a student staring at a blank page "thinking of an essay topic" is actually *waiting for inspiration* — not thinking — until they *actively* generate, evaluate, and organise ideas toward the goal of a thesis statement.
c12_ps_cbse_10_007	Students often believe **land reforms were a single, uniform Central law applied equally across India**. In reality: (1) Land is a **State List subject** (Entry 18, List II) — each state enacted its own Zamindari Abolition Act, Tenancy Act, and Ceiling Act with *different definitions* of "family," *different ceiling limits* (e.g., 10 acres in Kerala vs. 54 acres in Rajasthan for irrigated land), and *different exemptions* (plantations in Assam/Kerala, orchards in HP). (2) They confuse **"land reforms" with only "land redistribution"** — ignoring that tenancy reform (security, rent regulation) and consolidation were equally critical pillars. (3) They assume **judicial review struck down land reforms** — while courts did invalidate some early laws (e.g., *Kameshwar Singh v. State of Bihar* 1
c11_psy_cbse_07_002	Students believe "thinking in words" and "thinking in images" are mutually exclusive styles (verbalizer vs. visualizer). In reality, everyone uses both formats flexibly depending on task demands (e.g., mental rotation uses images; syllogistic reasoning uses propositions). This misconception arises from pop-psychology "learning styles" myths and leads students to misinterpret individual differences as fixed traits rather than strategic choices. Example wrong answer: "I'm a visual thinker so I can't do logic problems."
c12_ps_cbse_10_008	**Misconception**: “The Bombay Plan was a *government* plan, and all industrialists opposed planning.” **Reality**: The Bombay Plan was **drafted by private industrialists** (Tata, Birla, etc.) in 1944 — *before* Independence — and it **explicitly advocated state planning and a large public sector**. They did this because colonial India’s capital markets were too thin to fund the infrastructure (power, rail, steel) their own factories needed. **Students often confuse the *authors* (industrialists) with the *implementers* (Planning Commission), and assume “capitalists = anti-planning”.** In fact, the **only consistent anti-planning voices** in the 1950s were **liberal economists like B.R. c11_psy_cbse_07_003	Students believe "autistic thinking" refers to **Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD)** or clinical pathology. This is a terminology trap: in NCERT Class 11 Psychology, "autistic thinking" (from Bleuler's original term *autismus* meaning "self-referential") denotes a *normal cognitive mode* — fantasy, daydreaming, wish-fulfilling thought detached from reality-testing — present in all humans during creativity, dreaming, and play. It is NOT a symptom of ASD. Students write "autistic thinking is a disorder" in exams and lose marks because they import clinical psychology terminology into a cognitive psychology classification. The error stems from hearing "autistic" only in clinical contexts, not recognizing its historical cognitive psychology meaning.
c12_ps_cbse_10_009	Students often believe the "commanding heights" phrase comes from Lenin and was blindly copied by Nehru. In fact, the phrase was used by the Industrial Policy Resolution 1956 (Schedule A) and the Second Plan document — neither cites Lenin. The Indian list (17 industries) differs from the Soviet "commanding heights" (which included banking, foreign trade, and all large industry). The Indian state left banking private until 1969, foreign trade under state control but not public ownership, and allowed private steel (Tatas) and textiles. The misconception leads to answers that describe the Soviet model instead of the Indian mixed-economy variant.
c11_psy_cbse_07_004	Students believe "mental set" and "functional fixedness" are synonyms for "being stubborn" or "not thinking creatively." They incorrectly label any repeated error as mental set, and any unusual object use as overcoming functional fixedness. For example, a student who keeps using the quadratic formula for a factorable equation is showing mental set (procedural rigidity), but a student who fails to use a ruler as a straightedge because "it's for measuring" is showing functional fixedness (object-use rigidity). The core error is ignoring the *cognitive level*: mental set operates at the *strategy/procedure* level; functional fixedness operates at the *object representation* level.
c12_ps_cbse_10_010	Students often think Operation Flood was "just another government scheme like the Green Revolution" — i.e., a top-down programme where the state distributes inputs (cattle feed, crossbred cows) to farmers. In reality, the *state's role* was limited to creating NDDB and funding Phase I; the *entire procurement, processing, and marketing chain* was owned and run by producer cooperatives. The Green Revolution gave farmers seeds to use on *their own land*; Operation Flood gave landless herders a *collective enterprise* to own. This confusion leads students to attribute outcomes to "government subsidies" rather than "cooperative governance" — and miss why it empowered women (who managed cattle but never owned land) in a way land-title-based reforms never could.
c11_psy_cbse_07_005	Students often believe deductive reasoning is "always correct" and inductive reasoning is "just guessing." They fail to see that a deductive argument with a false premise (e.g., "All birds fly; Penguins are birds; Therefore penguins fly") yields a false conclusion despite valid logic, while a strong inductive argument (e.g., "The sun rose every morning for 10,000 years; therefore it will rise tomorrow") provides near-certain practical knowledge. This error arises from equating "deductive" with "true" and "inductive" with "weak," ignoring the distinction between validity/soundness and strength/cogency.
c12_ps_cbse_11_001	Students often equate **non‑alignment with neutrality or isolationism** — believing India "stayed out of everything." In reality, non‑alignment meant *active, independent engagement*: India condemned the 1956 Suez invasion (angering UK/France/US) but *did not* condemn the Soviet invasion of Hungary (angering the West), proving it took *issue‑based* positions, not a blanket "no comment." This misconception leads to wrong answers in board questions like "Non‑alignment meant India did not take sides in any conflict" (False — it took sides based on merit, not bloc loyalty).
c11_psy_cbse_07_006	Students often believe that "heuristic = bias" and that using heuristics means one is being stupid or lazy. In reality, heuristics are evolutionarily adaptive cognitive tools (Gigerenzer's "adaptive toolbox") that work well in many natural environments. The specific error is conflating the *mechanism* (heuristic) with the *outcome* (bias) only when the environment mismatches the heuristic's design. For example, a student writes: "The availability heuristic is a bias where you remember recent events." This is wrong because availability is the heuristic (retrieval fluency); the bias is the resulting overestimation of frequency. The student cannot distinguish the process from the error, leading to circular explanations in board answers.
c12_ps_cbse_11_002	Students often believe non-alignment meant India was "neutral" or "isolated" from world affairs. In reality, India was deeply engaged — mediating in Korea (1953), chairing the International Control Commission for Indochina (1954), leading the Suez protests (1956), and accepting aid from both US (PL-480 food aid) and USSR (Bhilai steel plant). Non-alignment was *active multi-alignment*: leveraging relationships with all powers to maximize autonomy, not withdrawing from the world.
c11_psy_cbse_07_007	Students often believe the incubation stage is simply "taking a break" or "procrastinating," and that illumination strikes randomly during this break. In reality, incubation *only* works after intense, focused preparation has loaded the problem into working memory; the unconscious recombination during incubation requires this saturated cognitive substrate. For example, a student who "incubates" a physics project by playing video games *without* first struggling with the design will not experience a useful illumination — the mind has no raw material to recombine.
c12_ps_cbse_11_003	Students often believe the 1962 war was fought *only* over the McMahon Line in the east (Arunachal). In reality, China’s primary strategic objective was securing the Aksai Chin road link between Xinjiang and Tibet — the western sector was militarily more critical for Beijing. The eastern offensive was a pressure tactic. This misconception leads to wrong answers like "China wanted Arunachal for territory" rather than "China wanted Aksai Chin for connectivity." Also, students confuse the 1962 ceasefire line with the current LAC — China withdrew to *pre-war* positions in the east but *retained* Aksai Chin, creating the status quo that defines today’s LAC.
c11_psy_cbse_07_008	Students equate "creative thinking" with "artistic talent" or "unconstrained wild ideas." Consequently, they dismiss their own ideas as "not creative enough" during brainstorming, violating Osborn's deferred judgment rule. They also confuse incubation with procrastination—thinking "taking a break" means passive phone scrolling rather than deliberate problem-loading followed by low-cognitive-load activity (walking, showering) that permits unconscious restructuring.
