c6_civics_ch16_041	Students often think "the economy" only refers to large banks or stock markets and ignore their own daily lives. They fail to see that a public park or a government school is a direct result of the government's economic role, not just a "gift."
c6_economics_ch07_001	Students often confuse "infrastructure" with "manufacturing machines." They might think that a loom in a textile factory is infrastructure. This happens because both help in production, but infrastructure is the *foundation* (like electricity or the building itself) while the machine is a *tool* used within that system.
c6_economics_ch07_002	Students often think infrastructure is only for "big cities" or "governments" and does not apply to their own lives. They may view a road as just a "path" rather than a critical economic tool. This happens because they see these items daily and take them for granted, failing to link them to the concept of "economic activity."
c6_economics_ch07_003	Students often think "infrastructure" only means things made of concrete and steel, like roads or bridges. They mistakenly classify a school building as "physical infrastructure" because it is a physical object. They fail to realize that social infrastructure is defined by its *purpose*—supporting human well-being—rather than the materials used to build it.
c6_economics_ch07_004	Students often believe that transport is only about "traveling" for leisure, rather than an economic necessity for moving goods. They fail to see that a truck carrying steel is an economic activity just as much as a farmer growing wheat.
c6_economics_ch07_005	Students often think that because the internet is "digital," it is not an economic activity. They confuse "economic activity" with only "making physical products" like cars or wheat. They fail to see that providing the connection to the internet is a service that is paid for, just like a bus ride or a doctor's visit.
c6_economics_ch07_006	Students often think infrastructure is only about big government projects (like airports) and do not realize that local things like village roads or power lines are also infrastructure. They fail to see that every small road link is part of the national economic chain.
c6_economics_ch08_001	Students often think a bank is just a "vault" or a big safe that holds cash. They fail to understand the "lending" part of the business, believing the bank's only job is to protect their bills.
c6_economics_ch08_002	Students often think banks generate money out of thin air to give to borrowers. They don't realize the money lent to borrowers is actually the money deposited by the savers.
c6_economics_ch08_003	Students often think interest is a "fixed" amount regardless of the principal, like a flat fee. They fail to realize it is a percentage, meaning the more money involved, the larger the interest payment or reward becomes.
c6_economics_ch08_004	Students often think all bank accounts earn high interest and are exactly the same. They believe that putting money in a Current Account is the same as a Savings Account, ignoring that Current Accounts are for businesses with high transaction volumes and typically offer no interest.
c6_economics_ch08_005	Students often think a "Cheque" or a "Debit Card" *is* the money itself. They think if they lose the card or the paper, they have lost their actual wealth. In reality, these are just "keys" or "instructions" to access the money stored in the bank account.
c6_economics_ch08_006	Students often believe that banks keep every customer's money in a separate personal drawer in the back. This is incorrect because it ignores the reality that banks pool money to make large investments or loans. They fail to realize that the "money" you deposit is actually used by the bank to fuel other people's economic activities.
c6_economics_ch11_001	Students often think barter means "selling things for a cheaper price." They confuse the *method* of payment (goods vs. money) with the *value* of the item. They might say, "I bartered my old toy for a new one," when they actually meant they just traded items; they fail to realize that barter is a system that *replaces* money, not just a way to get a discount.
c6_economics_ch11_002	Students often think that if two people have valuable items, a trade *must* happen. They forget that the specific *desire* for that specific item is the missing piece. For example, a student might think a person with gold will automatically get rice from a farmer, forgetting the farmer might already have enough gold and only wants a tractor.
c6_economics_ch11_003	Students often think money has always been "government-issued paper." They struggle to realize that anything can be money if a community agrees on its value. For example, they might think shells "lost their value" because they weren't "official," failing to see that the community's trust was the original "official" stamp.
c6_economics_ch11_004	Students often think money has value because of the paper it is printed on. In reality, money has value because society agrees it is a medium of exchange. They confuse the physical object (the note) with the economic function (the agreement to trade).
c6_economics_ch11_005	Students often think digital money is "fake" money because they cannot touch it. They believe that if they cannot hold it, it has no value, failing to realize that money is a system of accounting and trust, not just a physical object.
c6_economics_ch11_006	Students often believe that "saving" is only for rich people who have "extra" money. They assume that if you earn just enough for food and rent, you cannot save. This is a misconception because saving is a habit of setting aside a small percentage, regardless of the income level, to build security over time.
c6_economics_ch12_001	Students often believe a market must be a physical place they can visit. They think if they cannot walk into a building, it is not a market. This happens because they see physical markets (like vegetable stalls) daily but rarely think of digital platforms as "marketplaces."
c6_economics_ch12_002	Students often confuse "market size" with "shop size." They might think a large supermarket in their neighborhood is a "national market" just because it is big. It is actually a local market because it serves the immediate neighborhood.
c6_economics_ch12_003	Students often think that "high demand" automatically means "high price" regardless of supply. They fail to realize that if supply is *also* extremely high (e.g., a bumper crop of onions), the price might stay low even if many people want to buy them.
c6_economics_ch12_004	Students often think "competition" means the sellers are fighting or hurting each other. In reality, in economics, competition is a neutral mechanism where sellers try to attract customers by being better or cheaper. They confuse "fighting" with "competing for customer preference."
c6_economics_ch12_005	Students often confuse "consumer rights" with "being rude to shopkeepers." They think being an "aware" consumer means arguing or fighting with a seller. In reality, being aware means being informed and assertive about standards, not aggressive.
c6_economics_ch12_006	Students often believe that "markets" only refer to physical locations like the vegetable market or a grocery store. They fail to see that paying for a bus ticket, a haircut, or an online app subscription is also a market transaction because they do not see an exchange of a physical item.
c6_english_u1_001	Students often think the "setting" is only the weather or the scenery (e.g., "it is sunny"). They fail to realize that setting includes the *atmosphere* or *feeling* of a place that affects what a character can do (e.g., a quiet river allows for deep thought, whereas a loud market would not).
c6_english_u1_002	Students often confuse a character's "wishes" with their "personality traits." For example, they might say "Jahnavi is educated" because she wants to be, rather than saying "Jahnavi is ambitious" because she *seeks* education despite her poverty.
c6_english_u1_003	Students often confuse the "Topic" (e.g., "Bananas" or "Gold") with the "Theme" (e.g., "The value of hard work"). They might say the theme of a story is "farming," when the theme is actually "the reward of persistence." This happens because topics are concrete and easy to name, while themes require abstract thinking.
c6_english_u1_004	Students often think "persistence" means doing the exact same thing over and over again without changing. In reality, the spider (and Bruce) succeed because they keep trying *until* they succeed, often learning from each fall.
c6_english_u1_005	Students often confuse metaphors with similes. They think any comparison is a metaphor, even when it uses "like" or "as." For example, if a student writes "He is like a lion," they call it a metaphor, but it is actually a simile because of the word "like."
c6_english_u1_006	Students often confuse "descriptive poetry" (imagery) with "narrative poetry" (storytelling). They assume that because a poem has words and imagery, it must be a story, failing to realize that narrative poetry requires a sequence of events that change the situation of the characters.
c6_english_u1_007	Students often think context clues must be a direct definition (like "A plantation is a place where..."). In reality, clues are often indirect, like synonyms, descriptions of actions, or the general mood of the scene. If a student ignores action words, they miss the meaning entirely.
c6_english_u1_008	Students often mistake pronouns for nouns because they both occupy the subject position in a sentence. For example, they might call 'He' a noun because it acts like a person in the sentence, forgetting that 'He' is just a placeholder, not the actual name (the noun).
c6_english_u1_009	Students often mistake descriptive writing for a list of adjectives. For example, they might write, "The dog is big, brown, fast, furry, and loud," which is just a list. Descriptive writing should link these qualities to an action or a sensory experience to create a scene.
c6_english_u1_010	Students often think "listening" is just the absence of talking. They wait for their turn to speak rather than actively processing the speaker's message. For example, when a peer talks, the student prepares their own reply instead of listening to the peer's specific details.
c6_english_u2_011	Students often think "humour" only means "telling a joke." They fail to see that humour can also come from a situation being strange (absurdity) or when characters act in ways that are the opposite of what we expect (role-reversal).
c6_english_u2_012	Students often confuse 'feelings' with 'traits.' A feeling is temporary (like feeling sad because of a rainstorm), but a trait is a lasting part of a personality (like being 'cheerful' even when it rains). For example, a student might say, "Dr. Dolittle is happy because he is talking to a parrot," instead of identifying his 'curiosity' as a permanent trait.
c6_english_u2_013	Students often think empathy is just "being nice." They confuse being polite with the deeper work of empathy, which involves actively trying to understand a perspective that is foreign to their own. For example, they might think giving a sad friend a candy is empathy, but if they don't actually listen to why the friend is sad, they haven't achieved true empathy.
c6_english_u2_014	Students often think humour is only about "funny words" (like adjectives) rather than the "funny action" (the plot or situation). For example, if a poem says "The silly man ate a hat," a student might focus on the word "silly" rather than the fact that eating a hat is an absurd action.
c6_english_u2_015	Students often think "rhyme" just means any two words that sound vaguely similar, like "cat" and "car," or they think "repetition" must happen in every single line. This stems from a lack of focus on the *exact* ending sound or the *deliberate* choice of the poet.
c6_english_u2_016	Students often try to make all five lines the same length or ignore the rhythm entirely. They forget that lines 3 and 4 must be "bouncy" and short, resulting in a poem that sounds like a regular paragraph rather than a humorous song.
c6_english_u2_017	Students often guess the meaning of a word based on its "sound" or by picking the first synonym they find in a dictionary without checking if it fits the sentence. For example, if a text says, "The mahout was concerned about Gajaraj," they might choose "interested" instead of "worried," ignoring that the context mentions the elephant not eating.
c6_english_u2_018	Students often add "-ed" to every verb to make it past tense, regardless of whether it is regular or irregular (e.g., saying "eated" instead of "ate"). They do this because they learn the "-ed" rule first and try to apply it as a universal shortcut.
c6_english_u2_019	Students often think dialogue needs to be a "transcript" of every word said in real life, including "um," "ah," and boring greetings. This makes writing tedious and slow. They forget that dialogue in stories should only include the parts that help the story move forward or reveal a personality trait.
c6_english_u2_020	Students often think "recitation" is just memorizing lines and saying them as fast as possible to show they know the poem. They fail to realize that recitation is a *performance* where rhythm and pauses are as important as the words themselves. For example, a student might rush through a line like "The wind whispered softly" without actually letting the "whisper" sound soft.
c6_english_u3_021	Students often confuse "plot" (the full story) with "sequence" (the specific order of time). They may try to summarize the story by jumping from the start to the end, missing the middle inventions that define Anand's character. They think sequence is just a list, not a chain of reactions.
c6_english_u3_022	Students often confuse "what a character does" with "who a character is." They might say "Anand is an inventor" instead of identifying the trait of "curiosity." This happens because they focus on the plot event rather than the underlying personality.
c6_english_u3_023	Students often believe that "innovation" only refers to high-tech, expensive machines or gadgets. They fail to realize that innovation is a mindset of questioning and improving things, which can be applied to simple household chores or school projects.
c6_english_u3_024	Students often think a poem is only about what is physically happening (literal level). For example, they might say "The child likes flowers," missing that the flowers are "cargo" for a dream. They focus on the action instead of the symbolic meaning behind the action.
c6_english_u3_025	Students often confuse "Personification" with "Simile" (a comparison using 'like' or 'as'). For example, they might think "The tree stood tall like a soldier" is personification, but it is a simile because it uses "like." Personification MUST state the object *is* doing the action (e.g., "The tree guarded the house").
c6_english_u3_026	Students often believe that if it doesn't rhyme, it isn't "really" a poem. This happens because they are taught early on to associate poetry exclusively with nursery rhymes or songs, leading them to ignore the "art of the image" in non-rhyming verse.
c6_english_u3_027	Students often assume a word has only one "correct" dictionary definition and try to force that meaning into every sentence. For example, if they know 'bark' means a dog's sound, they might get confused when reading about 'neem bark' (the outer layer of a tree). They fail to realize that context determines which definition is appropriate.
c6_english_u3_028	Students often think all words ending in '-ly' are adverbs, or they try to use adjectives where adverbs are needed (e.g., "He ran fastly" or "He ran quick"). They confuse the form of the word with its function in the sentence.
c6_english_u3_029	Students often confuse "creative writing" with "making up lies" or "writing nonsense." They believe that because it is creative, they don't need to base it on reality, which leads to disjointed stories. For example, they might write about a tree that suddenly turns into a spaceship without any logical flow.
c6_english_u3_030	Students often confuse "presenting an idea" with "telling a story." They think if they speak for a long time about their topic, they are presenting, but they fail to include logical structure or supporting evidence. For example, a student might say "Neem is great because my grandma loves it" instead of "Neem is useful because it has medicinal properties that fight germs."
c6_english_u4_031	Students often think the "plot" is just a list of everything a character does, including unimportant things like eating or sleeping. They fail to realize that plot is specifically the sequence of important events that build toward a conflict or change.
c6_english_u4_032	Students often confuse "actions" with "traits." For example, they might say "Suraj is a train-watcher" instead of saying "Suraj is curious." They focus on the *what* instead of the *why* because they haven't learned to interpret behavior as evidence of personality.
c6_english_u4_033	Students often believe that "adventure" is only about physical travel to new places (like mountains or space). In reality, adventure is about the mindset of exploring the unknown, whether it is a dark room, a new school, or a difficult challenge.
c6_english_u4_034	Students often confuse personification with simply describing an object's function. For example, they might say "The car drives fast" is personification because the car is "driving." This is wrong because "driving" is what a car does naturally; personification requires an action *only* a human would do, like "The car groaned with exhaustion."
c6_english_u4_035	Students often think "imagery" must include all five senses at once. They struggle to realize that even one strong visual description is a form of imagery. For example, if a poem says "the blue sky," they might say "that's not imagery because I can't smell or hear it," failing to recognize sight as a sensory experience.
c6_english_u4_036	Students often mix up the word count or the part of speech for the middle (4th) line. They may write adjectives instead of nouns or use the wrong number of words, usually because they prioritize the rhyme (which is not required) over the strict structural "formula" of the diamante.
c6_english_u4_037	Students often try to guess a word's meaning by looking only at the word itself rather than the full sentence. They might assume 'hopeless' always means "sad," whereas in the sports unit, it specifically refers to "lack of skill." This happens because they are accustomed to memorizing single definitions rather than analyzing the author's intent.
c6_english_u4_038	Students often think that any long sentence is "complex." They confuse length with structure, often misidentifying a simple sentence with a long prepositional phrase (e.g., "Prabhat played a long match with his friend in the field") as complex because it contains many words.
c6_english_u4_039	Students often believe that "adventure" means constant action without any pause. They fill the story with running and fighting, forgetting that suspense comes from the quiet moments of waiting or exploring before the action happens.
c6_english_u4_040	Students often believe that "reading aloud" means reading every word at a constant, robotic speed without any pauses. This happens because they focus entirely on word recognition rather than understanding the character's intent. For example, they might read a line about a person being out of breath with the same steady, calm rhythm they use for a normal sentence.
c6_english_u5_041	Students often think a letter is just a formal document for information. They struggle to write "as themselves," often switching into "teacher-mode" or "textbook-mode" where they use complex, dry sentences instead of the natural, friendly voice used in the chapter.
c6_english_u5_042	Students often think sacrifice only means "dying in a war." This is a narrow view because it ignores the long years of hard work, time away from families, and the constant readiness to serve that soldiers display daily.
c6_english_u5_043	Students often confuse the National War Memorial with India Gate itself, thinking they are the same thing. This happens because they are geographically close and both relate to military history. Students need to understand that India Gate is a war memorial from an earlier era (WWI), while the National War Memorial is a newer, distinct site specifically for independent India's soldiers.
c6_english_u5_044	Students often confuse "subject" with "emotion." For example, they might say the "emotion" of the poem is "a soldier," which is actually the "subject." They do this because they are used to identifying nouns rather than feelings. They need to learn that "soldier" is who it's about, but "pride" is how it feels.
c6_english_u5_045	Students often think "repetition" means the same thing as "rhyme." They confuse the sound of the end of a line (rhyme) with the actual repeating of a word or phrase throughout the poem (repetition).
c6_english_u5_046	Students often write the vertical word but then write sentences that have nothing to do with that word, or they repeat the word itself in every line. This happens because they focus entirely on the "puzzle" of the letters rather than the "poetry" of the content. For example, if the word is "TREE," they might write "T-Top, R-Red, E-Eat, E-End" instead of describing a tree.
c6_english_u5_047	Students often mistake 'sacrifice' as only meaning "losing something," without understanding the "greater cause" element. For example, a student might say "I made a sacrifice when I dropped my ice cream," failing to see that 'sacrifice' in this unit requires a noble purpose or benefit to others.
c6_english_u5_048	Students often think that any sentence with the word "by" is automatically passive, or that passive voice is "wrong." This happens because they focus on the "by" marker rather than looking at whether the subject is performing the action. For example, "I sat by the river" has "by," but it is NOT passive because the subject (I) is performing the action (sat).
c6_english_u5_049	Students often mix up "salutations" (greetings) and "closings." For example, they might write "Dear Principal" (formal) but close with "See you later, bye!" (informal). This happens because they view the letter as one big block rather than a structured piece of communication where the tone must remain consistent from start to finish.
c6_english_u5_050	Students often treat group discussion as a "debate" where they must prove they are right. This leads to interrupting others or ignoring their points. They forget that the goal is to build understanding, not to "win."
c6_geography_ch01_001	Students often confuse "geographical diversity" with "political diversity" (like different states or languages). They assume that because India has many states, those states must have different geographies, even if they are neighbors. This happens because children learn about state borders before they learn about physical landforms.
c6_geography_ch01_002	Students often believe the Himalayas were formed by a single massive explosion or volcanic event. In reality, they are "fold mountains" formed by a slow, continuous "crushing" process, similar to pressing play-dough together from two sides.
c6_geography_ch01_003	Students often think the Northern Plains were "always there" as a flat surface, rather than being built up by rivers over millions of years. They assume land is static, leading them to miss that the rivers are the active "builders" of the region.
c6_geography_ch01_004	Students often confuse the Peninsular Plateau with the Himalayas, assuming all high land in India is a "mountain." This happens because students link "high altitude" only to "mountains," failing to recognize the flat, broad-topped nature of a plateau.
c6_geography_ch01_005	Students often think the entire Indian coastline is one uniform strip of land. They fail to realize that the Western and Eastern sides are separated by different mountain ranges and vary significantly in width and climate. For example, they might mistakenly assume the Western coast is wide and flat like the Northern Plains.
c6_geography_ch01_006	Students often confuse the location of the two island groups, frequently swapping the Arabian Sea for the Bay of Bengal. This happens because they visualize the map as a single block rather than identifying the two distinct bodies of water on either side of the Indian peninsula.
c6_geography_ch01_007	Students often believe deserts are just "hot sand" and that no one lives there. They fail to realize that the Thar is a culturally rich region where people have developed specific survival strategies for centuries, such as specialized housing and agricultural techniques.
c6_geography_ch02_008	Students often think climate is just "what the weather is like" without realizing the 30-year requirement. They might say, "The climate is cold" after only visiting a place for two days. They fail to realize that climate is a statistical average, not a momentary experience.
c6_geography_ch02_009	Students often believe the liquid "gets hot" and therefore moves. The misconception is that the liquid is reacting to its own heat, rather than expanding because of the energy transfer from the environment. They fail to distinguish between the object being measured (the air) and the mechanism of the tool (the liquid expansion).
c6_geography_ch02_010	Students often believe that a rain gauge measures the total volume of rain that falls on an entire city (like 'gallons' or 'buckets'). In reality, it only measures the 'depth' of the rainfall at one specific, small location, which acts as a sample for the surrounding region.
c6_geography_ch02_011	Students often believe that "wind creates pressure," when it is actually the opposite: pressure differences create wind. They think the wind pushes the pressure around, rather than air molecules moving to fill the space where pressure is lower.
c6_geography_ch02_012	Students often think a thermometer measures "how hot the sun is," rather than the temperature of the air around us. They make this mistake because they focus on the heat source rather than the local atmospheric condition being measured.
c6_geography_ch02_013	Students often think that "weather" is just whether it is sunny or rainy. They fail to realize that factors like wind direction, cloud type, and temperature ranges are equally important parts of a complete weather picture. They tend to record only the most obvious event (rain) and ignore the subtle changes that precede it.
c6_geography_ch02_014	Students often think weather is only about temperature (hot or cold). They fail to realize that weather also includes wind, humidity, and rainfall, which are equally vital for daily life. For example, a student might say "It's not hot, so the weather is fine," ignoring that high winds might be dangerous for travel.
c6_geography_ch03_015	Students often use the terms "weather" and "climate" interchangeably. They believe that because it is cold today, the "climate" is cold, failing to realize that climate is the *average* pattern over decades, not a single day's experience.
c6_geography_ch03_016	Students often believe that the monsoon is just "rainy clouds" that appear out of nowhere. They fail to realize that the wind *must* change direction to bring the moisture from the ocean. Without the pressure difference created by the hot land, those clouds would never be "pulled" over the country.
c6_geography_ch03_017	Students often think "Summer" is the only time the sun is hot, failing to realize that "Pre-monsoon" or Summer is specifically defined by high heat combined with dry air. They also frequently confuse the timing of harvest cycles with the wrong season.
c6_geography_ch03_018	Students often think crops can grow anywhere if farmers just "work hard enough." They fail to realize that climate is a biological limit, not just a preference. For example, they might think rice can grow in the Thar Desert simply because someone could carry water there, ignoring that the heat and humidity levels are entirely different from the natural habitat required for the plant.
c6_geography_ch03_019	Students often assume that all deserts are hot. They associate the word "desert" only with sand and heat (like the Thar), failing to realize that a desert is technically defined by a lack of precipitation, which allows cold regions like Ladakh to be classified as "cold deserts."
c6_geography_ch04_020	Students often think agriculture appeared everywhere in India at the exact same time. They assume that because they learn about the "Indus Civilisation" first, everyone was farming by 2600 BCE, which ignores the thousands of years of earlier development that started in the northwest.
c6_geography_ch04_021	Students often believe that commercial farming only exists in Western countries or that it must involve modern machinery. They fail to realize that commercial farming is defined by the *intent* (selling for profit) and *scale* (large surplus), which is a common practice in many parts of India, such as sugarcane or tea farming.
c6_geography_ch04_022	Students often think all crops grow year-round regardless of rainfall or temperature. They assume a farmer can grow rice in a desert simply by wanting to, ignoring the biological limit of the plant for specific water levels.
c6_geography_ch04_023	Students often think all crops grow year-round if given enough water. They forget that temperature is a critical "gatekeeper"—a heat-loving crop like rice will not thrive in the cold winter, regardless of how much water it gets.
c6_geography_ch04_024	Students often think "Modern Farming" is just about tractors. They overlook that without irrigation and fertilizers, a tractor alone cannot increase crop yields. They fail to see that these three elements (Water, Nutrients, Machines) form a linked chain.
c6_geography_ch04_025	Students often believe that "more chemicals = more food," assuming that chemical fertilizers are always better than natural methods. They make this error because they see advertisements for fertilizers or notice how fast crops grow initially, ignoring the long-term "soil degradation" that makes the land unproductive later.
c6_geography_ch05_026	Students often confuse the placement of the "Seven Sisters" states in the Northeast with the borders of Myanmar and Bangladesh. They often think Myanmar is to the North instead of the East. This happens because the map of Northeast India looks complex, and students struggle to orient themselves when the land curves.
c6_geography_ch05_027	Students often think a border is a physical fence or wall that looks the same everywhere. They fail to realize that borders follow natural landscapes; for example, the Himalayas *are* the border with China. This leads to the error of assuming that all borders are flat lines on the ground.
c6_geography_ch05_028	Students often confuse "cultural links" with "political alliances" or "trade agreements." They assume that because countries are neighbours, they must have political treaties, ignoring the fact that these cultural ties are about shared beliefs and history, not government policies.
c6_geography_ch05_029	Students often think trade is just "selling" things to others. They fail to realize that India also "imports" or buys goods from its neighbors, like agricultural products or electricity, because it is more efficient than producing everything alone.
c6_geography_ch05_030	Students often think "neighbours" must touch the land border of India. They struggle to understand that countries separated by water are still neighbors. They might mistakenly assume only countries like Pakistan or Nepal are "neighbours" because they are visible on a land map.
c6_geography_ch05_031	Students often think "geopolitical significance" means military power or fighting, but in this context, it refers to the importance of LOCATION for trade and connectivity. They confuse "strategic location" with "having a strong army."
c6_history_ch04_001	Students often assume early humans "decided" to build cities overnight. They miss the gradual process where small farming villages slowly expanded as they traded more goods and created better tools. This is a common error because students are used to seeing cities already built and fully functional today.
c6_history_ch04_002	Students often confuse the "discovery" of the civilisation (1920s) with the "existence" of the civilisation (2600 BCE). They might assume that because we only found it recently, it must be a modern invention or not very old.
c6_history_ch04_003	Students often assume that all ancient cities were disorganized or "messy" because they think "old" equals "primitive." They may struggle to believe that people living thousands of years ago could create perfectly straight streets. This happens because students associate technology solely with computers and modern machinery.
c6_history_ch04_004	Students often think Harappans were just "farmers" like the earlier Neolithic people. They fail to realize that the "urban" or "city" aspect of the Harappans was possible because they had moved beyond simple farming into organized, specialized work like pottery and textile production.
c6_history_ch04_005	Students often assume the Great Bath was an Olympic-style swimming pool for sports. They project modern leisure activities onto the past because they cannot imagine other reasons for such a large water structure.
c6_history_ch04_006	Students often think the Harappan Civilisation was "destroyed" or "conquered" in a single war because they equate "decline" with "being defeated." In reality, the evidence points to a long, slow process of environmental stress. They confuse the gradual fading of a culture with the sudden end of a battle.
c6_history_ch05_007	Students often assume that the Mauryan Empire appeared suddenly in an empty, uninhabited land. This is incorrect because the subcontinent was already full of organized communities and small kingdoms (mahajanapadas) for a long time.
c6_history_ch05_008	Students often think Ashoka stopped being a king or lost his empire after he gave up war. They confuse "non-violence" with "abdication" or "weakness." They assume that if you don't fight, you can't be a leader.
c6_history_ch05_009	Students often think Ashoka carved these edicts only to brag about his victories. In reality, the edicts focus heavily on his regret over the Kalinga War and his desire for peace. Students confuse the edicts with a "trophy room" of a king, failing to understand they were a revolutionary way to promote social ethics.
c6_history_ch05_010	Students often think the Emperor personally managed every village and district. They fail to realize that the *amatyas* acted as the bridge, implementing the central government’s policies locally, which prevented the system from being overwhelmed by the sheer size of the empire.
c6_history_ch05_011	Students often think Ashoka "forced" people to become Buddhists. However, Ashoka used moral persuasion and public messaging, not violence. Students make this error because they associate "Emperors" and "Power" with force, failing to realize Ashoka’s conversion followed his rejection of war after Kalinga.
c6_history_ch05_012	Students often assume the Mauryan Empire was "conquered" by an outside force, when in fact, the text notes it declined due to weak leadership and was replaced by an internal general (Pushyamitra Shunga). They miss that internal political decay is just as important as external invasion.
c6_history_ch05_013	Students often confuse the Gupta Empire with the Mauryan Empire because both have kings named "Chandragupta." They think they are the same time period. This happens because they don't look at the dates (320 CE vs. the earlier period).
c6_history_ch05_014	Students often assume Harsha was an ancient king from the same time as the Buddha or Ashoka. In reality, he lived much later (7th century CE). This confusion happens because students lump all "great kings" into one general "ancient" time period.
c6_history_ch06_015	Students often believe that "Medieval" means the time before humans had technology or settled life. This is a confusion with the "Stone Age" or "Ancient" history. They assume all historical periods before the present are the same "olden days."
c6_history_ch06_016	Students often think "Bhakti" is just a new type of ritual. They struggle to understand that it is actually the *removal* of rituals. They might think, "Oh, they just changed the songs," instead of realizing they changed the whole relationship between the person and God.
c6_history_ch06_017	Students often think Sufis were just "hermits" who lived alone in caves. This is incorrect because they actually lived in communities called khanqahs and actively interacted with and guided the public.
c6_history_ch06_018	Students often assume that Islam spread only through "conquest" because they conflate the arrival of the faith with the later establishment of large empires. They fail to realize that trade networks existed for centuries before any political expansion, making the "trader" path just as significant as the "general" path.
c6_history_ch06_019	Students often think "Rajput" refers to a single family or a single king who ruled all of India. In reality, the Rajputs were a collection of many different clans (Chauhans, Tomars, Rathores) ruling independent territories in the North.
c6_history_ch06_020	Students often think "medieval" means "primitive" or "without progress." In reality, this period saw massive advancements in how people expressed their identity through local languages and engineering feats like the Brihadisvara Temple.
c6_history_ch07_021	Students often think Qutbuddin Aibak conquered India all by himself as an independent king from the start. They miss the fact that he was a general under Muhammad of Ghur and only became the Sultan *after* his leader's death. This is common because they often simplify history into "one hero" stories rather than seeing the transition of power.
c6_history_ch07_022	Students often think the Delhi Sultanate was a single "kingdom" ruled by one king for 300 years. They fail to realize that a "dynasty" change often meant a violent or political shift where one royal family was replaced by another. This leads to confusion when they see multiple names like "Aibak" and "Khalji" as if they were related.
c6_history_ch07_023	Students often believe the Sultan did all the work by himself because he was the "supreme authority." They fail to see that "supreme" means he has the final say, not that he performs every task alone. For example, they might think the Sultan personally drafted every letter, ignoring the existence of the Diwan-i-Insha.
c6_history_ch07_024	Students often believe that "arch and dome" means the Sultanate builders brought their own finished stones from Central Asia. In reality, they used local Indian stone and local workers but taught them new ways to assemble them.
c6_history_ch07_025	Students often think that because the state was Islamic, everyone in the territory was forced to convert to Islam. This is incorrect because the sheer size of the population and the political reality made total conversion impossible and impractical for the Sultans to maintain order.
c6_history_ch07_026	Students often think the Delhi Sultanate ended abruptly with Timur’s invasion. In reality, the Sultanate continued for over a century under the Sayyid and Lodi dynasties, but it was just a shadow of its former self. Students make this error because they associate a "sack" or "massacre" with the immediate end of a civilization.
c6_history_ch08_027	Students often mistakenly think that the Vijayanagara Empire was the only kingdom in India at the time. This happens because textbooks often isolate chapters; in reality, India was home to many diverse regional kingdoms existing simultaneously, as explored in the "Many in the One" theme of this chapter.
c6_history_ch08_028	Students often think the Bahmani Kingdom and the Deccan Sultanates existed at the same time as separate competing countries. This is incorrect because the Sultanates are the *result* of the Bahmani Kingdom's breakup, not its rivals.
c6_history_ch08_029	Students often assume that all Rajputs belonged to one single ruling family or dynasty. In reality, "Rajput" was a broad category for many different clans (like the Chauhans, Rathores, and Sisodias) who were rivals as often as they were allies.
c6_history_ch08_030	Students often think the Maratha Kingdom appeared instantly as a large empire. In reality, it was a slow process of capturing one fort at a time and gathering local support, not a single conquest.
c6_history_ch08_031	Students often confuse the Sikh Gurus with the political rulers like Ranjit Singh. They assume that because the religion was founded by a Guru, all subsequent leaders were religious heads. It is crucial to distinguish between the religious leadership of the Gurus and the political leadership of Ranjit Singh who unified the state.
c6_history_ch08_032	Students often think that "regional" means "unimportant" or "divided." They assume that because kingdoms were separate, they had no connection to each other. In reality, these kingdoms were like different branches of the same tree; they had local variety but shared deep, common Indian roots.
c6_history_ch09_033	Students often think Babur was already a powerful Indian King who just took over Delhi. In reality, he was an outsider from Central Asia who had to fight his way into India. They make this error because they associate the "Mughals" so strongly with Indian history that they forget the empire began as a foreign arrival.
c6_history_ch09_034	Students often think Akbar inherited a stable empire and just kept it that way. In reality, he inherited a fragile, shrinking empire after his father's sudden death, and he had to work to build its strength from a state of vulnerability.
c6_history_ch09_035	Students often assume the Emperor did all the work personally because they read he had "absolute authority." This is wrong because they confuse "having the final say" with "performing every task." In reality, absolute authority required a massive support system to execute orders across the empire.
c6_history_ch09_036	Students often confuse Mughal architecture with generic "ancient Indian" temple architecture. They assume all stone buildings in Indian history were built by the Mughals, failing to distinguish between the arch/dome style of the Mughals and the pillar/beam style of earlier periods.
c6_history_ch09_037	Students often assume that because the Mughal Empire was "big" under Aurangzeb, it was at its strongest. They fail to realize that territorial size does not equal internal stability, especially when religious policies create friction within the population.
c6_history_ch09_038	Students often think the Mughal Empire was purely a military state and ignore the "everyday" economy. They believe that because the Emperor was powerful, the economy was only about tax collection, forgetting that artisans and merchants were the backbone of urban life.
c6_history_ch10_039	Students often think "factory" meant a modern building with machines. In the 17th century, a "factory" was just a warehouse or a trading station for storing goods before shipment. If they think of smoke-filled chimneys, they miss the point that these were simply storage and office hubs for merchants.
c6_history_ch10_040	Students often think the British won because they were "more modern" or "smarter" than the Indians. This is incorrect; the British won because they used local political instability and greed to their advantage. They didn't win by being better; they won by being more manipulative.
c6_history_ch10_041	Students often think the British took over India purely because they were 'stronger' in every way. In reality, the British were successful because they exploited existing rivalries between Indian rulers and used treaties to divide and conquer, not just through superior weapons.
c6_history_ch10_042	Students often think the revolt was purely a "military mutiny" about gun parts. In reality, while the cartridges were the immediate trigger, the soldiers were also frustrated by broader colonial policies. Focusing only on the grease makes it seem like a small accident rather than a planned protest against foreign rule.
c6_history_ch10_043	Students often think the East India Company and the British Government were the same entity from the beginning. They assume the British Raj existed from the moment the first trader arrived. This is wrong because the Company was a private business group that only lost its power to the Crown after the 1857 Revolt.
c6_history_ch10_044	Students often assume that "cheap cloth" was a "good deal" for Indians without realizing that the destruction of the local textile industry caused massive unemployment. They focus on the price of the product rather than the loss of the worker's income and skill.
c6_history_ch11_045	Students often think nationalism happened instantly or that everyone in India agreed on everything from day one. In reality, it was a gradual process where people had to overcome differences in language and region to find a common voice.
c6_history_ch11_046	Students often think Non-Cooperation meant attacking British soldiers. This is incorrect because it confuses "non-cooperation" with "armed rebellion." The movement was specifically designed to be non-violent to show the moral strength of the Indian people.
c6_history_ch11_047	Students often think the Civil Disobedience Movement was a small, secret group of people sneaking around to make salt. In reality, it was a massive, open public protest meant to be seen and joined by thousands of people to show the British that their laws were losing authority.
c6_history_ch11_048	Students often think the Quit India Movement happened because India was already at war with Britain. Actually, it was a political movement launched because of the *failure* of diplomatic talks (Cripps Mission) while Britain was busy with World War II.
c6_history_ch11_049	Students often think Bose was "against" Gandhi, implying personal hatred. In reality, they shared the same goal of a free India but disagreed on the methods. Thinking they were enemies prevents students from understanding the complexity of the freedom movement where different methods coexisted.
c6_history_ch11_050	Students often think the British government "split" India just to be mean or cause trouble. In reality, the partition was a political outcome resulting from specific demands by the Muslim League and the subsequent acceptance by Congress, rather than a top-down British decision alone.
c6_history_ch12_051	Students often think the Constitution was written by a single person, like Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, acting alone. They overlook the fact that 299 members of the Constituent Assembly worked together to represent the entire nation's interests.
c6_history_ch12_052	Students often think all princely states were forced into India by military power alone. In reality, the vast majority joined through negotiations and agreements signed by the rulers. They make this error because they often hear about the few difficult cases (like Hyderabad or Junagadh) and assume that was the standard process for all 500+ states.
c6_history_ch12_053	Students often think "Economic Planning" means the government controlled every single person's job or personal spending. In reality, it was about the government investing in big projects like dams, irrigation, and steel plants to build the foundation for the country's future.
c6_history_ch12_054	Students often confuse "mixed economy" with "having no money" or "only government control." They mistakenly believe that because Nehru was the leader, he controlled every single shop and farm in India.
c6_history_ch12_055	Students often assume that all conflicts after 1947 were against the same enemy (Pakistan). In reality, India faced different challenges from different borders, and ignoring the 1962 war with China overlooks a critical moment in Indian history where India realized it was unprepared for a multi-front threat.
c6_history_ch12_056	Students often think that the name 'India' was the original name of the land, whereas it is actually a name derived from the river 'Sindhu' used by foreigners. They fail to realize that 'Bhārata' is the native, more ancient term.
c6_math_ch01_001	Students often believe that "estimation" is just a wild guess with no logical basis. For example, when asked to estimate the number of breaths in an hour, a student might just say "100" without considering that we breathe roughly 15-20 times per minute. They fail to link the estimate to a smaller, known quantity.
c6_math_ch01_002	Students often believe that 0 is a natural number because they see it on a number line alongside 1, 2, and 3. This leads to errors when counting objects or categorizing sets. They forget that natural numbers are strictly for "counting things" (you cannot count "zero" apples in your hand).
c6_math_ch01_003	Students often confuse the digit itself (face value) with its contribution to the total number (place value). For example, in 3,042, a student might say the place value of 0 is 0, which is correct, but they might struggle with 3,402 and say the 4 is worth 400 because they "see" it near the front, forgetting that the 0 occupies a place that must be accounted for.
c6_math_ch01_004	Students often compare the "size" of the numbers by looking only at the first digit they see (from left to right) without checking the number of digits first. For example, they might wrongly claim 900 is larger than 1,000 because 9 > 1.
c6_math_ch01_005	Students often try to place commas every three digits (e.g., 10,000,000 instead of 1,00,00,000) because calculators and computers often default to the international format. This leads to confusion when reading numbers in Indian textbooks or newspapers.
c6_math_ch01_006	Students often try to round by looking at the wrong digit, such as rounding 167 to the nearest ten by looking at the 1 instead of the 7. This happens because they do not realize the "neighboring digit to the right" is the only one that dictates the change.
c6_math_ch01_007	Students often try to subtract any smaller number from any larger number, such as writing 95 as "VX" (100-5) or 99 as "IC" (100-1). This is incorrect because Roman numerals only allow specific subtractive pairs (like IV, IX, XL, XC, CD, CM) based on powers of ten.
c6_math_ch01_008	Students often forget to include the "carried" digit when summing the next column. For example, in 45,678 + 23,456, when adding the tens column (7+5), they get 12 and write 2, but then add 6+4 in the hundreds column and get 10, forgetting to add the 1 carried from the previous step. This happens because they view each column as an isolated problem.
c6_math_ch01_009	The "Always Subtract Smaller from Larger" error: Students often subtract the smaller digit from the larger digit regardless of whether it is on top or bottom (e.g., in 52 - 18, they do 8 - 2 = 6, then 5 - 1 = 4, resulting in 46 instead of 34). This happens because they prioritize speed over the rule that the top number must be greater than the bottom number to perform simple subtraction.
c6_math_ch01_010	Students often forget to include the "placeholder" zero when multiplying by the tens digit. For example, in 123 × 21, they might write 123 × 1 = 123 and 123 × 2 = 246, then add 123 + 246 = 369. This happens because they view digits as isolated symbols rather than values based on their position (20 instead of 2).
c6_math_ch01_011	Students often "drop" a number and forget to place a placeholder zero in the quotient. For example, in 816 / 8, they might incorrectly write 12 instead of 102. This happens because they focus only on the digit they brought down and ignore the value of the place they are currently filling.
c6_math_ch01_012	Students often round the wrong digit or "double round" (e.g., rounding 4,499 to 5,000 because 4,499 is close to 4,500). They should focus only on the digit immediately to the right of the target place value, regardless of the other numbers in the set.
c6_math_ch01_013	Students often confuse factors and multiples, thinking that because 2 × 6 = 12, then 12 is a factor of 2. They mistake the product (multiple) for the divisor (factor).
c6_math_ch01_014	Students often try to apply the "last digit" rule (used for 2 and 5) to the number 3. For example, they might think 313 is divisible by 3 because 3 is at the end, ignoring that the sum of digits is 7.
c6_math_ch01_015	Students often stop factorising too early, such as writing 12 = 3 × 4 and claiming they are done. They forget that 4 is a composite number that can be split further into 2 × 2. This happens because they view factorisation as just "any multiplication" rather than specifically "prime multiplication."
c6_math_ch02_016	Students often believe that -10 is "bigger" than -1 because 10 is bigger than 1. This happens because they focus only on the numeral (the magnitude) and ignore the negative sign, which flips the relationship of the numbers.
c6_math_ch02_017	Students often believe that since 5 is bigger than 2, then -5 must be bigger than -2. They focus on the magnitude of the digit and ignore the negative sign, failing to realize that on the number line, -5 is to the left of -2, making it smaller.
c6_math_ch02_018	Students often treat negative numbers like positive ones, assuming that because 10 is larger than 5, -10 must be larger than -5. This happens because they see the "10" and "5" and ignore the negative sign, which acts as a "direction" indicator on the number line.
c6_math_ch02_019	Students often confuse the sign of the sum when adding a positive and a negative number. They might calculate (+3) + (-7) and get +4, simply subtracting the smaller from the larger and keeping the first number's sign, or they might ignore the negative sign entirely. This happens because they are still thinking in terms of primary school "take away" subtraction rather than directional movement.
c6_math_ch02_020	Students often treat the subtraction sign as a "remove" instruction only, failing to realize that subtracting a negative number acts like adding. They often calculate 3 - (-2) as 1 because they subtract the 2 from the 3, ignoring the negative sign in the middle.
c6_math_ch02_021	Students often believe that the additive inverse of a negative number must also be negative. For example, they might say the additive inverse of -8 is -8. This happens because they associate "inverse" only with the action of "making something negative," failing to see it as a "balancing" action that must result in zero.
c6_math_ch02_022	Students often mistakenly apply the addition rule for signs to multiplication. For example, they might think $(-3) \times (-4) = -7$ because they are "combining" the negative values, or they assume the result must be negative because the inputs are negative.
c6_math_ch02_023	Students often apply the "two negatives make a positive" rule to addition instead of multiplication and division. For example, they might solve (-10) / (-2) correctly as 5, but then think (-10) + (-2) is also 5. This happens because they memorize "negative + negative = positive" as a blanket rule for all operations.
c6_math_ch02_024	Students often try to apply the commutative and associative properties to subtraction and division (e.g., thinking 10 - 5 = 5 - 10). This happens because they over-generalize the rules they learned for addition and multiplication to all operations.
c6_math_ch02_025	Students often believe that vertical bars act like a "negative" sign, turning positive numbers into negative ones. For example, they might think |5| = -5. This happens because they see the bars and feel forced to "do something" to the number, often confusing this with the rule for multiplying by a negative sign.
c6_math_ch02_026	Students often believe that -10 is "larger" than -2 because 10 is a larger number than 2. This happens because they see the negative sign as just a symbol and focus only on the magnitude (the digit).
c6_math_ch02_027	Students often fail to cross the zero barrier correctly. For example, in the sequence 2, 0, -2, ..., they might guess "0" or "1" next, because they treat the "negative" numbers as if they behave like positive numbers (thinking -2 comes after -3 in magnitude). They struggle to visualize that -4 is "further" from zero than -2.
c6_math_ch02_028	Students often confuse the "sign of the number" with the "operation to perform." For example, if asked to subtract -5 from 2, they may write 2 - 5 instead of 2 - (-5). They do this because they see the minus sign in front of the 5 and assume it is the only sign that matters, forgetting that the context of "subtracting" a debt is fundamentally an addition of value.
c6_math_ch03_029	Students often think a larger denominator means a larger fraction (e.g., thinking 1/8 is bigger than 1/4 because 8 is bigger than 4). This happens because they focus on the number in the denominator rather than the size of the "share" created by division.
c6_math_ch03_030	Students often try to convert improper fractions to mixed numbers by simply placing the smaller number over the larger number regardless of which was originally the numerator. For example, converting 8/3 to 3 2/3 instead of 2 2/3. This happens because they focus on "fitting the numbers together" rather than performing the division of the total parts by the denominator.
c6_math_ch03_031	Students often try to find equivalent fractions by adding the same number to both the numerator and denominator (e.g., changing 1/2 to 2/3). This is wrong because fractions represent ratios, and addition does not preserve the proportion of the parts to the whole.
c6_math_ch03_032	Students often believe that the fraction with the larger denominator is always the larger fraction (e.g., thinking 1/9 > 1/5 because 9 > 5). This happens because they see 9 as a "bigger number" than 5, forgetting that in fractions, the denominator represents the number of pieces the whole is cut into, meaning more pieces equals smaller pieces.
c6_math_ch03_033	The most common error is "denominator addition," where students add numerators and add denominators (e.g., 1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5). This happens because students apply the rules of whole number addition to both parts of the fraction without realizing that the denominator represents the "name" or "size" of the unit, not a quantity of items.
c6_math_ch03_034	Students often subtract the numerators and the denominators separately (e.g., 3/4 - 1/2 = 2/2). This happens because they treat fractions as two independent whole numbers rather than a single value representing a part of a whole.
c6_math_ch03_035	Students often try to find a common denominator before multiplying, just as they do with addition and subtraction. For example, in 1/2 × 1/3, they might change it to 3/6 × 2/6 and then mistakenly multiply the numerators to get 6/6 (or 1), ignoring that the denominator should also be multiplied.
c6_math_ch03_036	Students often try to divide the numerators and denominators separately (e.g., 4/5 ÷ 2/3 = 2/1.66) or simply multiply across without flipping the divisor. This happens because students over-generalize the "multiply across" rule they learned for simple multiplication of fractions.
c6_math_ch03_037	Students often treat the "marks" on a number line as the numbers themselves rather than the "gaps" between the marks. For example, when asked to mark 3/4, they count the 0 as the "first" mark and place their dot on the 3rd mark total, which is actually 2/4. They fail to realize that the fraction represents the distance (the interval), not the tick mark itself.
c6_math_ch03_038	Students often confuse the "share" with the "whole." For example, if asked to find 2/3 of 12, they might answer 2 or 3 because they see those numbers in the fraction, rather than understanding that 12 must be partitioned into 3 parts. This happens because they try to perform operations on the numbers they see without visualizing the "part of a whole" concept.
c6_math_ch03_039	Students often compare the sizes of fractions by only looking at the digits. For example, they believe 1/8 > 1/3 because 8 is greater than 3. They treat the numbers as independent integers rather than as parts of a divided whole, forgetting that the denominator represents the number of slices—the more slices you make, the smaller each slice must be.
c6_math_ch03_040	Students often believe the larger number must always be the denominator (the bottom number), thinking $3/4$ is correct but $4/3$ is "impossible." This arises from seeing fractions only as "parts of a whole" rather than "division."
c6_math_ch03_041	Students often add or subtract numerators and denominators separately (e.g., 1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5). This happens because they treat fractions as two independent whole numbers instead of a single value representing a part of a whole.
c6_math_ch04_042	Students often think that 0.4 is smaller than 0.25 because they see "4" and "25" and assume 25 is bigger. They treat the digits after the decimal point as whole numbers rather than parts of a whole (tenths/hundredths).
c6_math_ch04_043	Students often treat the digits to the right of the decimal point as whole numbers, believing that 0.45 is larger than 0.6 because "45 is bigger than 6." This happens because they ignore the place value (tenths vs. hundredths) and only look at the face value of the digits.
c6_math_ch04_044	Students often think a longer decimal is always larger (e.g., 0.125 > 0.2) because they treat the decimal part like a whole number, ignoring that the first digit after the decimal point represents tenths, which is the most significant part.
c6_math_ch04_045	Students often divide the larger number by the smaller number regardless of whether it is the numerator or the denominator. For example, when asked to convert 1/4, they calculate 4 ÷ 1 = 4 instead of 1 ÷ 4 = 0.25.
c6_math_ch04_046	Students often align numbers to the right (like whole numbers) instead of aligning the decimal point. For example, calculating 2.5 + 1.23 as 3.73 (correct) vs 2.5 + 1.23 = 1.48 (by adding 2 to 1 and 5 to 23). This happens because they forget that 2.5 is actually 2.50.
c6_math_ch04_047	Students often try to align decimal points vertically as they do in addition. They don't realize that in multiplication, the decimal places "shift" and combine. For example, in 0.2 x 0.3, they might write 0.6 instead of 0.06 because they don't count the total decimal places.
c6_math_ch04_048	Students often try to "move the decimal" only in the dividend or forget to move it in the dividend after moving it in the divisor. For example, in 4.5 ÷ 0.5, they might incorrectly calculate 4.5 ÷ 5 = 0.9. They treat the decimal point as a static object rather than a indicator of place value that must be shifted consistently.
c6_math_ch04_049	Students often treat the digits after the decimal point as whole numbers, such as thinking 0.50 is "fifty" and 0.5 is "five," leading them to believe 0.50 is larger than 0.5. This happens because they view the decimal part as an independent whole number rather than a fraction of the unit.
c6_math_ch04_050	Students often try to round by looking at the very last digit in a long decimal (e.g., rounding 3.472 by looking at the 2 instead of the 7). They mistakenly think all digits to the right contribute to the "round up" decision.
c6_math_ch04_051	Students often "align digits to the right" instead of aligning the decimal points. For example, when adding 1.25 and 0.5, they write 0.5 under 25, resulting in 1.75, which is correct, but if they add 1.25 and 0.05, they might align the 5s and get 1.30 instead of 1.30. This error happens because students treat decimals like integers without respecting the positional value of tenths, hundredths, and thousandths.
c6_math_ch05_052	Students often confuse the "coefficient" (the number attached to a variable, like 5 in 5x) with the "variable" itself. They might say "5x is the variable," when only 'x' is the variable and 5 is a constant acting as a multiplier.
c6_math_ch05_053	Students often mistakenly include the plus or minus sign as a separate "operation" rather than part of the term itself, or they treat the variable as part of the coefficient. For example, in 5x - 3y, they might identify the coefficient of the second term as 3 instead of -3, or identify 'x' as part of the coefficient 5.
c6_math_ch05_054	Students often confuse the placement of terms in subtraction and division. For example, when asked for "5 less than x", they write $5 - x$ instead of $x - 5$. This happens because they read left-to-right exactly as the words appear, ignoring that the "starting" quantity must come first in the expression.
c6_math_ch05_055	Students often try to add variables as if they were just numbers, leading them to claim $5x + 2 = 7x$. They ignore the fact that the '2' does not have an 'x' attached, treating the constant as if it belongs to the variable family.
c6_math_ch05_056	Students often forget to perform the same operation on both sides of the equation. For example, in 3x + 2 = 8, they might subtract 2 from the left side but forget to subtract it from the 8, resulting in 3x = 6 instead of 3x = 6. This happens because they view the equals sign as a "go to the answer" arrow rather than a balance scale.
c6_math_ch05_057	Students often "move" a term to the other side without changing its sign (e.g., changing $3x - 5 = 10$ to $3x = 10 - 5$ instead of $3x = 10 + 5$). This happens because they view the equals sign as a "go" sign rather than a scale that requires inverse operations (adding/subtracting) to maintain balance.
c6_math_ch05_058	Students often confuse "3 times more than x" (which is 3x + x or 4x) with "3 times x" (3x). They also struggle with "less than," often writing 5 - x instead of x - 5 when told a number is 5 less than x.
c6_math_ch05_059	Students often try to "move" a number to the other side by changing its sign without performing the balance operation (e.g., changing $2x + 3 = 7$ to $2x = 7 + 3$ instead of $2x = 7 - 3$). They view the equals sign as a "gate" to jump over rather than a balance point, which leads to sign errors.
c6_math_ch05_060	Students often try to find the rule by looking at the relationship between the term and the position as an addition problem instead of a multiplication problem. For example, in 2, 5, 8..., they see $2+3=5$, so they might guess the rule is $n+3$, ignoring that the pattern must work for all terms, not just the first two.
c6_math_ch05_061	Students often treat variables as specific objects (e.g., thinking "$x$" stands for "apple") rather than as numbers. This leads to errors like saying $3x + 2 = 5x$ because they think "$x$" is a label. They fail to realize that $x$ is a number that, once found, makes the mathematical statement true.
c6_math_ch06_062	Students often forget to convert units before writing a ratio, or they treat a ratio like a set of independent numbers. For example, when comparing 1 kg of rice to 500 grams of dal, a student might write 1:500 instead of 1000:500 (or 2:1).
c6_math_ch06_063	Students often try to add the same number to both parts of a ratio to find an equivalent ratio (e.g., changing 2:3 to 3:4). This is incorrect because addition changes the proportional relationship, whereas only multiplication or division preserves it.
c6_math_ch06_064	Students often confuse which number to divide by which. For example, if 4 pens cost 20 rupees, they might calculate 4 ÷ 20 = 0.2 instead of 20 ÷ 4 = 5. They treat the numbers as isolated digits rather than "Total Cost" and "Total Quantity."
c6_math_ch06_065	Students often try to use addition instead of multiplication. For example, if 2 pens cost 10 rupees, they might think 4 pens cost 12 rupees (adding 2 to the price) instead of 20 rupees (multiplying by 2). This happens because they view the relationship as a simple sequence rather than a proportional ratio.
c6_math_ch06_066	Students often try to use the "cross-multiplication" method from direct proportion ($a/b = c/d$) for inverse problems. They do this because they are used to solving ratios and forget that in inverse proportion, the *product* stays the same, not the ratio. For example, if 2 workers take 4 days, they might incorrectly think 4 workers take 8 days ($2/4 = 4/8$).
c6_math_ch06_067	Students often mistake part-to-part for part-to-whole by using the second part of the ratio as the denominator. For example, if given 5 apples and 10 oranges, they might say the ratio of apples to total fruit is 5:10 instead of 5:15. This happens because they see two numbers and automatically put them in a fraction without summing them to find the "whole."
c6_math_ch06_068	Students often try to solve proportion problems by adding the same number to both sides of a ratio instead of multiplying/dividing. For example, if 2:3 = 4:x, they might think x = 5 (adding 2 to each side). This ignores the multiplicative nature of ratios.
c6_math_ch06_069	Students often use addition instead of multiplication when solving proportions. For example, in the juice problem (2:5), they might think "I added 4 to the 2, so I add 4 to the 5," resulting in 2:9 instead of 6:15. This happens because they see the numbers as a sequence rather than a multiplicative relationship.
c6_math_ch07_070	Students often confuse a line with a line segment because they see a drawing of a line on a page and assume it is finite because the paper ends. They think that because they can't see the line extending forever, it must stop at the page edge.
c6_math_ch07_071	Students often believe that if two lines are "close" to each other but don't touch on the paper, they are parallel. They fail to realize that if they were to extend them, they might cross. For example, they might label two lines that form a very thin 'V' shape as parallel because the gap is small.
c6_math_ch07_072	Students often think the size of an angle changes if you extend the length of the arms. For example, they might claim that a 30° angle with 5cm arms is smaller than a 30° angle with 10cm arms. This happens because they perceive the visual space between the endpoints of the arms rather than the amount of rotation at the vertex.
c6_math_ch07_073	Students often mistakenly believe that if a triangle is "equilateral" (all sides equal), its angles must also be different sizes. They fail to realize that equal sides imply equal turns (angles) at the corners. For example, they might guess an equilateral triangle has angles of 50, 60, and 70 degrees.
c6_math_ch07_074	Students often believe that if a shape has four equal sides, it MUST be a square. They forget about the rhombus, which has four equal sides but lacks the 90-degree corner property.
c6_math_ch07_075	Students often believe that "regular" just means "symmetric" or "looks normal." For example, they might call a rectangle a regular quadrilateral because it looks neat and balanced. They miss that "regular" strictly requires all sides to have the same length, which a non-square rectangle lacks.
c6_math_ch07_076	Students often believe that any line segment drawn inside a circle is a diameter or a radius. They fail to realize that the radius MUST start at the center and the diameter MUST pass through the center. For example, a student might label a random short chord as a radius because they see it "inside" the circle.
c6_math_ch07_077	Students often confuse the 'face' of a 3D shape with its 'edge,' or they forget to count the 'hidden' faces and edges that are not visible from a single perspective. For example, when looking at a cube, a student might only count 3 faces because they only see the front, top, and side, failing to realize a solid object has 6 faces in total.
c6_math_ch07_078	Students often think a shape only has symmetry if it is "cut in half" by a vertical line. They fail to recognize horizontal or diagonal lines of symmetry because they are fixed on a top-to-bottom perspective. For example, they might say a rectangle has only one line of symmetry instead of two.
c6_math_ch07_079	Students often apply the "180-degree rule" to quadrilaterals or the "360-degree rule" to triangles. They treat the magic number (180 or 360) as a guess rather than a property of the shape's complexity.
c6_math_ch07_080	Students often try to draw the third side first by guessing its length or by using a ruler to "connect" the arcs without measuring them. They fail to realize that the intersection of the two arcs *automatically* defines the length of the third side, and they often assume they need to know the third side's length before starting.
c6_math_ch07_081	Students often fail to change the compass width after drawing the first arc, or they change the width mid-construction, which prevents the arcs from intersecting correctly. They mistakenly believe the compass width must be the same for all parts of the construction, whereas only the arcs from the two centers must share the same radius.
c6_math_ch07_082	Students often assume that ALL angles formed by a transversal cutting two parallel lines are equal. They see 8 angles and assume they are all the same, failing to distinguish between the acute and obtuse angles created.
c6_math_ch07_083	Students often confuse "congruent" with "similar." They think if shapes look alike (like two triangles of different sizes), they are congruent. This happens because they focus only on the "shape" and ignore the "size" requirement.
c6_math_ch07_084	Students often believe that the size of an angle changes if the arms (the lines forming the angle) are drawn longer. For example, they think a 30-degree angle with 5cm arms is "smaller" than a 30-degree angle with 10cm arms. They confuse "length" with "amount of turn."
c6_math_ch08_085	Students often add only two sides of a rectangle (length + width) and stop, forgetting that a rectangle has four sides (two lengths and two widths). They treat the perimeter as the sum of just the dimensions given in the problem statement rather than the full boundary.
c6_math_ch08_086	Students often confuse the formula for perimeter (2 × (l + w)) with the formula for area (l × w). They attempt to add the dimensions for area or multiply them for perimeter because they treat both formulas as "just some math rule" rather than understanding that perimeter measures lines (edges) and area measures squares (surface).
c6_math_ch08_087	Students often confuse Perimeter (the distance around) with Area (the space inside). They tend to apply the perimeter formula (2 × (l + w)) when asked for area, or vice-versa, because both involve length and width measurements. For example, for a 5 cm by 4 cm rectangle, they might answer 18 cm² (thinking of perimeter) instead of 20 cm².
c6_math_ch08_088	Students often use the length of the "slanting side" (the slanted edge of the parallelogram or triangle) as the "height." They do this because they confuse the boundary length with the perpendicular distance. For example, in a triangle with base 10 and sides 6 and 7, they might calculate $A = \frac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 6 = 30$, ignoring the fact that 6 is not the perpendicular height.
c6_math_ch08_089	Students often confuse the area of a circle (πr²) with the circumference (2πr). They might see a problem asking for the space covered by a circular rug and calculate the distance around the edge instead, leading to an incorrect result in linear units (cm) rather than square units (cm²).
c6_math_ch08_090	Students often try to include the "hidden" internal line where two shapes meet when calculating the perimeter. For example, if a 5x2 rectangle is joined to a 3x3 square, they might add all sides of both shapes (5+2+5+2 + 3+3+3+3), forgetting that the touching boundary is no longer part of the "outside."
c6_math_ch08_091	Students often confuse "Perimeter," "Area," and "Volume." They might try to add the dimensions (l + w + h) or multiply only two (l × w) when asked for volume. This happens because they are familiar with perimeter and area formulas and try to force those patterns into a 3D context.
c6_math_ch08_092	Students often confuse surface area with volume. They might try to multiply length x width x height instead of adding the areas of the faces. For example, for a 2x3x4 cuboid, they might calculate 24 instead of 2(6+8+12) = 52.
c6_math_ch08_093	Students often confuse "squaring" the radius (r × r) with "multiplying by two" (r × 2). For a radius of 3, they calculate 3 × 2 = 6 instead of 3 × 3 = 9. This happens because they over-generalize the "double" rule from the perimeter of a rectangle.
c6_math_ch08_094	Students often confuse "perimeter" and "area" because they both involve length and width. For example, when asked to find how much fence is needed, they might multiply the length and width (area) instead of adding them and doubling (perimeter). This happens because they focus on the numbers provided rather than the physical meaning of the task (lining the edge vs. filling the space).
c6_math_ch09_095	Students often fail to "group" tally marks correctly. When they reach 5, they often continue drawing vertical lines (`|||||`) instead of the standard cross-hatch (`||||` with a strike-through). This makes counting large numbers of tallies extremely difficult and prone to error.
c6_math_ch09_096	Students often "skip" the diagonal line for the fifth tally, simply drawing five vertical lines (`|||||`). This makes the data harder to read quickly, as the human eye struggles to distinguish groups of five without that diagonal break.
c6_math_ch09_097	Students often assume every symbol always represents exactly "1" unit, regardless of what the key says. For example, if the key says one symbol = 10, they will still count the symbols as "1, 2, 3..." instead of "10, 20, 30...". This happens because they are conditioned to count objects one-by-one in early primary school.
c6_math_ch09_098	Students often start the vertical axis at a number other than zero or use inconsistent spacing between numbers (e.g., 0, 5, 20, 25). This makes the graph look "stretched" or "shrunken" in parts, which distorts the data and makes it impossible to compare the bars accurately.
c6_math_ch09_099	Students often try to add the values of the two side-by-side bars together. They confuse the double bar graph with a "stacked" bar graph and assume the total height of both bars combined is the value they need to report.
c6_math_ch09_100	Students often ignore zeros in a data set when calculating the mean (e.g., thinking 0, 5, 10 mean = 15/2 instead of 15/3). They treat '0' as "no value" rather than a valid data point that affects the count.
c6_math_ch09_101	Students often try to find the median without sorting the numbers first. For example, in the set {5, 1, 9}, they might pick 1 because it is in the middle of the original list. They make this error because they view the list as a static sequence rather than a collection of values to be organized.
c6_math_ch09_102	Students often choose the highest *numerical value* in the list as the mode instead of the *most frequent value*. For example, in the set 2, 2, 8, 8, 8, 9, they might pick 9 because it is the biggest number, ignoring that 8 appears three times while 9 appears only once.
c6_math_ch09_103	Students often mistake the "total outcomes" by only counting the outcomes that are different from the one they want.
