For example, a student might believe that Mahmud of Ghazni conquered and ruled over the interior of India just like the later Mughals, completely missing the reality that his primary objective was raiding wealth (especially temple treasures) rather than establishing a permanent empire in the Gangetic plains.
c7_hist_ch07_002	Students often think that Mahmud of Ghazni and Muhammad Ghori were rulers of the same dynasty with the exact same goal of founding a Muslim empire in India. For example, students frequently assume Mahmud stayed in India and ruled Delhi, confusing him with later Delhi Sultans. In reality, Mahmud was from Ghazni and only raided for wealth, whereas Ghori initiated permanent conquest.
c7_hist_ch07_003	Students often assume that all Rajput kingdoms formed a single, unified empire under one emperor, much like the Mauryas or Guptas, and therefore imagine that the 11th and 12th-century conflicts were simply "India versus invaders." In reality, northern India was divided among numerous independent, competing Rajput clans (such as the Chauhans of Ajmer, Chandellas of Bundelkhand, and Paramaras of Malwa) who frequently fought each other just as much as they resisted external foes.
c7_hist_ch07_004	Students often think that the Delhi Sultanate was a single, stable empire from 1206 CE onwards, missing the reality that early rulers spent decades fighting internal rebellions from Turkic nobles, regional Rajput resistance, and external Mongol threats while struggling to centralize power.
c7_hist_ch07_005	Students often assume that the 11th and 12th centuries were a time of total economic stagnation and declining trade because of political fragmentation and repeated foreign invasions. For example, they believe that Mahmud of Ghazni's raids completely ruined Indian internal and external commerce, ignoring the flourishing maritime trade along the coasts and the vibrant activities of powerful domestic merchant guilds.
c7_hist_ch07_006	Students often think that armies in the 11th and 12th centuries were identical to modern national armies with uniform salaries and government-issued uniforms. In reality, armies were feudal and coalition-based, consisting of personal retainers, temporary mercenaries, and regional lords who brought their own private forces to support the king.
c7_hist_ch07_007	Students often believe that the Delhi Sultanate was governed as a uniform, tightly-knit bureaucratic empire similar to modern nation-states or the later British Raj. In reality, it was a network of shifting military outposts and *iqtas* where local chiefs (*rais* and *ranas*) often retained autonomy as long as they paid annual tribute to the Sultan.
c7_hist_ch07_008	Students often assume that Indo-Islamic architecture appeared fully formed overnight with the arrival of Turkic rulers in the 12th century, believing that local Indian traditions were instantly replaced. In reality, the synthesis was a gradual, experimental process where local Indian artisans applied their traditional stone-carving skills to new structural forms like arches and domes over several decades.
c7_hist_ch07_009	Students often assume that the 11th and 12th centuries were an era of total cultural stagnation due to political conflicts and invasions, missing the vibrant growth of regional languages, architectural synthesis, and mathematical advancements that actually occurred during this period.
c7_hist_ch07_010	Students often think that the arrival of Turkic rulers in the 11th and 12th centuries caused an immediate and total replacement of Indian culture with foreign customs. For example, they believe that local art, music, and language disappeared overnight and were replaced entirely by Persian and Central Asian ways, ignoring the deep continuity and active synthesis of local traditions.
c7_hist_ch07_011	Students often think that the 11th and 12th-century invasions instantly and completely replaced existing Indian social structures with an entirely foreign system of life. For example, they might believe that villages overnight adopted new laws and customs, ignoring the deep-rooted continuity of village panchayats, caste structures, and agricultural practices that persisted despite changing political rulers at the top.
c7_hist_ch08_001	Students often believe that all people who arrived from outside India in ancient and medieval times were violent conquerors who forced local populations to convert or submit. For instance, students might confuse peaceful refugee groups like the Parsis or early Jewish and Christian traders with military invaders, failing to realize that the vast majority of migrant groups came seeking shelter, trade, or employment and peacefully integrated into local society.
c7_hist_ch08_002	Students often think that people migrated to India exclusively to conquer territory and establish political empires, failing to recognize that many groups arrived as peaceful refugees, religious exiles, or displaced merchants seeking only safety and a place to live. For example, students frequently confuse the military invasions of Central Asian rulers with the peaceful migrations of persecuted religious minorities like the early Parsis or Jews.
c7_hist_ch08_003	Students often confuse the Parsi migration with later mercantile migrations or British-era arrivals, assuming they came for trade under European protection. In reality, the earliest Parsis arrived centuries earlier as political and religious refugees escaping persecution in post-conquest Persia, landing on the Gujarat coast long before European trading companies reached India.
c7_hist_ch08_004	Students often believe that all Jewish people in India arrived at the exact same time during the British colonial period, similar to European traders. In reality, the earliest Jewish communities (like the Bene Israel and Cochin Jews) arrived over a thousand years before British rule, settling peacefully as merchants and refugees under indigenous Indian rulers.
c7_hist_ch08_005	Students often assume that Christianity in India was entirely introduced by Portuguese and British colonizers in the modern era, completely overlooking the ancient indigenous Christian communities (such as the Saint Thomas Christians) that existed in Kerala for over a thousand years before European ships reached Indian shores.
c7_hist_ch08_006	Students often think that Muslim communities remained entirely separate foreign groups in India, overlooking the deep localization, intermarriage, linguistic blending, and adoption of Indian customs that occurred over centuries. For instance, students might believe that Mughal clothing and food were imported directly from Central Asia without any Indian influence, ignoring how garments like the sherwani or culinary staples evolved specifically within the Indian climate and agricultural context.
c7_hist_ch08_007	Students often think that assimilation means foreign communities completely threw away their ancestral traditions the moment they landed in India, or conversely, that they lived in completely sealed, separate communities without any cultural exchange. For example, they might assume that Parsi or Jewish communities practiced zero local customs, ignoring how they adopted local attire, languages, and culinary practices while keeping their religious faith intact.
c7_hist_ch08_008	Students often believe that cultural contributions from migrant communities were forced upon the local population by rulers, thinking that local traditions were completely erased. In reality, cultural blending was a two-way, organic process of adoption and adaptation where both host and migrant communities influenced each other over generations.
c7_hist_ch08_009	Students often think that *Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam* meant that ancient Indian society had no social conflicts or prejudices, imagining a utopian paradise where everyone lived in complete harmony. In reality, while the philosophical ideal promoted universal brotherhood, historical societies still experienced caste hierarchies, political rivalries, and community tensions, even as they successfully integrated large waves of migrants.
c7_hist_ch08_010	Students often think that pluralism and tolerance in India mean people lived completely separate lives without interacting, or conversely, that everyone completely abandoned their distinct identities to merge into a single uniform culture. In reality, Indian pluralism historically involved "unity in diversity"—communities maintained distinct religious, linguistic, and cultural practices while engaging in deep everyday sharing of trade, music, art, and philosophical dialogue.
c7_math_ch01_001	Students frequently misplace commas or miscount zeros when writing and reading numbers involving lakhs, writing numbers like $10,0,000$ or confusing $1,00,000$ with $10,000$ because they forget that a lakh requires five zeros following the digit 1 in the Indian system.
c7_math_ch01_002	Students frequently misplace commas or misread 6 and 7-digit numbers by treating them like the International system (grouping by threes from the right: millions/billions) instead of the Indian system (grouping by threes first, then groups of two: Thousands, Lakhs, Crores). For example, when reading 4252389, they might write or read it as 4,252,389 instead of the correct Indian grouping 42,52,389. Another common error is omitting zero placeholders when converting expanded numbers like $7,00,000 + 50$ directly into standard form, writing 7,50 instead of 7,00,050.
c7_math_ch01_003	Students often misplace commas or misread numbers by treating all periods as groups of three digits (like the International system) or by forgetting placeholder zeros when converting words to digits. For example, when asked to write "Seven lakh five" in digits, a student might write 7,5 instead of 7,00,005 because they omit the empty Thousands, Hundreds, and Tens places.
c7_math_ch01_004	Students often write 8-digit numbers by inserting zeros incorrectly when a period is empty. For instance, when asked to write "Three crore four lakh", they write $3,40,00,000$ instead of $3,04,00,000$ because they confuse "four lakh" with "forty lakh" by misplacing the zero within the lakhs period.
c7_math_ch01_005	Students often compare large numbers by looking at the total number of digits ignoring place value alignment, or they look at the last few digits (units and tens) thinking larger ending digits make the entire number larger (e.g., believing 4,50,01,299 is greater than 4,50,02,100 because 99 is larger than 00).
c7_math_ch01_006	Students frequently look at the wrong digit when deciding whether to round up or down—for instance, looking at the digit in the units or hundreds place instead of the digit immediately to the right of the target place value. Another major error is keeping the trailing digits as non-zero numbers or forgetting to carry over when a 9 rounds up to a 10. For example, when rounding 4,96,000 to the nearest ten-thousand, students might write 4,90,000 instead of recognizing that the 9 in the ten-thousand place combined with the thousands digit causes a carry-over to the lakh place, making it 5,00,000.
c7_math_ch01_007	Students often look at the final digit or the largest digit of a number rather than the specific test digit immediately to the right of the target place value. For example, when rounding 4,382 to the nearest 100, a student might look at the units digit (2), see it is less than 5, and incorrectly reason about it instead of looking at the tens digit (8). Another frequent error is changing digits to the left of the target place value during the rounding process.
c7_math_ch01_008	Students often assume that number patterns in products continue purely by visual guesswork (e.g., adding zeros or sticking digits together) without checking the underlying place value arithmetic. For example, when multiplying $99 \times 99$, students might write $9999$ because they see two nines becoming four nines, completely ignoring actual multiplication rules and place value expansion.
c7_math_ch01_009	Students often misalign place value columns when setting up vertical addition or subtraction for large numbers (lakhs and crores) because they forget to right-align numbers of unequal digit lengths. For example, when adding $4,50,000$ and $2,50,00,000$, a student might align the leftmost digits ($4$ and $2$) instead of the rightmost digits, resulting in a nonsensical sum like $2,95,00,000$ instead of the correct sum of $2,54,50,000$.
c7_math_ch01_010	Students frequently mismanage "zero placeholders" during multi-step borrowing in subtraction with large numbers. For instance, when subtracting from a number like $5,00,00,000$, students often treat the internal zeros as $0$ instead of borrowing across them properly, or they forget to reduce a neighboring digit by $1$ after successfully borrowing, leading to off-by-one errors in multiple columns.
c7_math_ch01_011	Students frequently drop a place-holder zero in the quotient during long division when a brought-down digit is smaller than the divisor, or they misalign partial products during multi-digit multiplication. For example, when dividing 7,02,000 by 7, students often write the quotient as 1,030 instead of 1,00,300 because they skip recording the zero for the thousands and hundreds places when the digits are smaller than 7.
c7_math_ch02_001	Students often split an expression at every single operation symbol (+, -, ×, ÷), treating every number as its own term. For example, in $20 - 4 \times 3$, a struggling student might mistakenly think there are three terms ($20$, $4$, and $3$) and try to subtract before multiplying.
c7_math_ch02_002	Students often evaluate expressions strictly from left to right across all operation types, ignoring the priority of multiplication and division over addition and subtraction. For example, when evaluating $10 + 5 \times 2$, a student incorrectly adds $10 + 5 = 15$ first, then multiplies by $2$ to get $30$, instead of multiplying $5 \times 2 = 10$ first and then adding $10 + 10 = 20$.
c7_math_ch02_003	Students often evaluate expressions strictly from left to right across the entire string without respecting brackets or the order of operations, leading to incorrect comparisons. For example, when comparing $10 + 2 \times 5$ and $(10 + 2) \times 5$, a student might incorrectly calculate the left side as $(10 + 2) \times 5 = 60$ by rushing or adding first, missing that multiplication must occur before addition.
c7_math_ch02_004	Students often distribute a multiplier outside a bracket to only the first term inside the parentheses while ignoring subsequent terms, such as writing $3 \times (4 + 5)$ as $3 \times 4 + 5$ instead of $(3 \times 4) + (3 \times 5)$. Another common error is removing brackets preceded by a minus sign without changing the signs of the terms inside, such as writing $50 - (10 + 5)$ as $50 - 10 + 5$ instead of $50 - 10 - 5$.
c7_math_ch02_005	Students often perform operations from left to right across the entire expression, ignoring the boundary walls created by brackets. For example, in `50 - [ 20 + ( 5 × 2 ) ]`, a student will mistakenly calculate `50 - 20 = 30` first, completely ignoring the square and round brackets that demand `( 5 × 2 )` be computed first. Another common error is removing brackets prematurely without completing the inner operation, leading to sign and operation mix-ups.
c7_math_ch02_006	Students frequently apply the multiplier outside the parentheses to only the first term inside while completely forgetting to multiply it by the second term. For example, when evaluating $6 \times (20 + 4)$, a student might write $6 \times 20 + 4$ instead of $(6 \times 20) + (6 \times 4)$, resulting in an incorrect final calculation of $120 + 4 = 124$ instead of $120 + 24 = 144$.
c7_math_ch02_007	Students frequently omit necessary brackets when translating phrases containing "the sum of" or "the difference of" followed by multiplication or division. For example, when translating "Multiply 4 by the sum of 5 and 3", students often write $4 \times 5 + 3$ instead of $4 \times (5 + 3)$. This computational error happens because they translate words from left to right mechanically without considering that the addition must happen *before* the multiplication according to the sentence structure.
c7_math_ch02_008	Students frequently perform addition and subtraction before multiplication and division when scanning from left to right, or they evaluate multiplication before division purely because 'M' comes before 'D' in BODMAS. For example, in simplifying $20 - 4 \times 3 + 2$, a student might incorrectly calculate $20 - 12$ first or calculate $4 \times 3$ and then multiply instead of dividing when division appears first. Another major error is removing brackets from the outside in, rather than solving the innermost parentheses `()`, then curly braces `{}`, and finally square brackets `[]`.
c7_math_ch02_009	Students often assume that an expression containing larger individual numbers or more digits overall must always evaluate to a greater value, even when operations like subtraction or smaller multipliers alter the relationship. For example, when comparing $600 - 250$ and $580 - 210$, a student might mistakenly focus only on $600 > 580$ and conclude the first expression is larger, ignoring the larger amount being subtracted ($250 > 210$).
c7_math_ch02_010	Students often apply commutative or associative properties blindly to subtraction and division expressions, writing things like $15 - 8 = 8 - 15$ or treating $(12 \div 4) \div 2$ as equal to $12 \div (4 \div 2)$. Another common error is mixing up the distributive property with the associative property when parentheses are involved.
c7_math_ch03_001	Students often treat the smaller fractional parts (tenths, hundredths) as independent whole numbers rather than parts of a whole, leading them to write $3$ strips and $4$ parts as $34$ instead of $3\frac{4}{10}$. Another common error is believing that because 100 is greater than 10, a hundredth ($\frac{1}{100}$) is larger than a tenth ($\frac{1}{1010}$), ignoring the inverse relationship between the number of partitions and the size of each part.
c7_math_ch03_002	Students often write the fraction $\frac{1}{10}$ as decimal $0.01$ instead of $0.1$. This happens because they confuse the tenths place (the first position after the decimal point) with the hundredths place, thinking that the number of zeros in the denominator ($10$ has one zero) does not correspond directly to the decimal place value structure.
c7_math_ch03_003	Students frequently misinterpret the place value of zeros in decimals, writing $\frac{6}{100}$ as $0.6$ instead of $0.06$. They treat the numerator 6 as if it belongs directly next to the decimal point, ignoring the empty tenths place that requires a zero placeholder. Another common error is assuming that any number with more digits is larger, leading them to believe $0.125$ is greater than $0.2$ because 125 is greater than 2.
c7_math_ch03_004	Students often assume that numbers with more digits after the decimal point are always larger, or they misread place values by counting from right to left like whole numbers. For example, when comparing $0.45$ and $0.405$, a student might claim $0.405$ is larger because "four hundred five is bigger than forty-five," ignoring that the $4$ in both represents tenths, but the second number has a zero in the hundredths place making its hundredths value smaller.
c7_math_ch03_005	Students frequently misalign place values when converting mixed sub-units directly into a single decimal number, writing $5\text{ kg } 8\text{ g}$ as $5.8\text{ kg}$ instead of $5.008\text{ kg}$. They treat the smaller unit number ($8$) as a tenths or hundredths value without accounting for the power of ten required by the conversion factor ($1000\text{ g} = 1\text{ kg}$), ignoring intermediate zero place holders.
c7_math_ch03_006	Students often miscount the tick marks on a number line because they count the *lines* (lines drawn) rather than the *spaces* (intervals between lines), or they confuse the start of the interval. For example, when locating $1.3$ between $1$ and $2$, a student might count the tick for $1$ as "one" and end up placing $1.3$ on the mark meant for $1.2$ or $1.4$, failing to realize that the starting integer $1$ is the baseline ($1.0$) and the first tick to the right is $1.1$.
c7_math_ch03_007	Students often ignore place value length and compare decimals as if they were whole numbers based on the digits after the decimal point (e.g., concluding that $14.2$ is smaller than $14.15$ because $2$ is smaller than $15$). Another common error is failing to align the decimal points or pad with trailing zeros, leading to false conclusions about tenths and hundredths magnitudes.
c7_math_ch03_008	Students frequently misalign decimal numbers by right-justifying them as if they were whole numbers (treating $12.4 + 3.15$ as $12.4 + 31.5$ by lining up the 4 and the 5), ignoring the position of the decimal point. Another common error is failing to carry over correctly across the decimal point when the sum of tenths exceeds 10.
c7_math_ch03_009	Students often align decimals by the right edge (like whole numbers) instead of aligning the decimal points, writing $14.2 - 3.56$ as $14.2 - 3.56$ aligned on the right, which incorrectly matches tenths with hundredths. Another common error is failing to add placeholder zeros, leading them to drop digits down directly (e.g., $5.4 - 2.13$ becomes $3.33$ because they drop the $3$ straight down from the hundredths place).
c7_math_ch03_010	Students often drop trailing zeros or misalign decimal places when converting fractions with powers of 10, or they write the decimal digits directly as the numerator without matching the place value denominator. For example, when converting $0.07$ to a fraction, students frequently write $\frac{7}{10}$ instead of $\frac{7}{100}$ because they ignore the zero placeholder in the tenths place.
c7_math_ch03_011	Students often assume that place values to the right of the decimal point increase in magnitude as the digits get larger numerically, or they treat the decimal part as a separate whole number (e.g., thinking 0.45 is greater than 0.5 because 45 is greater than 5). Another common error is multiplying or dividing by powers of 10 by simply adding or removing zeros without tracking the movement of the decimal point relative to place value columns.
c7_math_ch04_001	Students frequently confuse variables with constants or labels, treating a letter like $a$ as an abbreviation for an object (e.g., thinking $a$ stands for "apples" rather than "the number of apples"). For example, when asked to write "There are 5 more pens than pencils," where pencils are $p$ and pens are $n$, a student might incorrectly write $p + a = n$ or treat letters as literal units like $5p$ meaning "5 pens" instead of $5 \times p$. Another severe error is assigning an arbitrary fixed value to a variable immediately (e.g., deciding $x$ always equals 1 because it is the first letter).
c7_math_ch04_002	Students frequently drop the negative sign when identifying coefficients of terms that follow a subtraction sign, or they confuse the constant term with coefficients. For example, in the expression $3x^2 - 5x + 7$, a student will often say the coefficient of $x$ is $5$ instead of $-5$, ignoring the minus sign that belongs to the term.
c7_math_ch04_003	Students often distribute a multiplier to only the first term inside parentheses or fail to distribute a negative sign correctly across all terms. For example, when simplifying $-2(3x - 4)$, students frequently write $-6x - 4$ instead of the correct $-6x + 8$, forgetting that multiplying a negative number by a negative number yields a positive product.
c7_math_ch04_004	Students frequently misinterpret verbal phrases involving subtraction and division by reversing the order of terms. For example, in the phrase "decrease $x$ by 7", students often write $7 - x$ instead of $x - 7$, or when seeing "divide 20 by $y$", they write $y \div 20$ instead of $\frac{20}{y}$. This happens because students read words sequentially from left to right without analyzing the directional relationship of the mathematical action.
c7_math_ch04_005	Students often assume that if a single shape takes $k$ matchsticks, then $n$ connected shapes will always take $k \times n$ matchsticks, completely ignoring the fact that connected shapes share sides. For example, if one square takes 4 matchsticks, students write $4n$ for $n$ squares, failing to realise that sharing sides means subsequent squares only require 3 additional matchsticks, making the correct expression $3n + 1$.
c7_math_ch04_006	Students frequently commit the "exponent addition error" when combining like terms with powers, writing $3x^2 + 5x^2 = 8x^4$ instead of $8x^2$. They mistakenly treat addition of like terms the same way they treat multiplication of terms with exponents, forgetting that variables and their exponents represent scaling factors rather than repeated multiplication when combined additively. Another major error is combining constants with variable terms, such as simplifying $4x + 3$ into $7x$.
c7_math_ch04_007	Students frequently add or multiply the variables themselves along with the coefficients, or they combine terms with different exponents (e.g., treating $x$ and $x^2$ as like terms, writing $3x + 2x^2 = 5x^3$). Another frequent error is ignoring the operational sign directly in front of a term, such as treating $-3x$ as a positive $3x$ when rearranging expressions.
c7_math_ch04_008	Students often set the coefficient of $n$ equal to the first term of the sequence instead of the common difference between consecutive terms. For example, given the sequence 5, 8, 11, 14, a student might write $5n$ instead of $3n + 2$, thinking the multiplier must match the starting number.
c7_math_ch04_009	Students frequently omit multiplication signs or parentheses when substituting negative numbers or coefficients. For example, when evaluating $5 - 2x$ for $x = -3$, students often write $5 - 2-3$ instead of $5 - 2(-3)$, leading them to subtract instead of multiplying $-2$ by $-3$ to get $+6$.
c7_math_ch04_010	Students often look at the common difference in a geometric pattern (e.g., adding 3 matchsticks each step) and write down only $3n$, completely ignoring the starting fixed number of elements present in Step 1. For example, if Step 1 has 5 matchsticks and increases by 3 each step, students write $3n$ instead of $3n + 2$, failing to test their expression with $n = 1$.
c7_math_ch05_001	Students often confuse the "point of intersection" with the endpoints of line segments or think that intersecting lines can have multiple crossing points without curving. For example, when shown two intersecting lines, a student might point to the ends of the drawn segments instead of the central crossing point, or they might believe two straight lines can loop around and intersect twice like a figure-eight.
c7_math_ch05_002	Students frequently confuse the linear pair sum property ($180^\circ$) with complementary angles ($90^\circ$) or full-turn angles ($360^\circ$). When solving algebraic equations like $4x + 20 = 180$, they often subtract $20$ from $180$ correctly to get $160$, but then divide by $4$ incorrectly or mistakenly add the coefficient to $180$, writing $4x = 200$ instead of $4x = 160$.
c7_math_ch05_003	Students frequently confuse vertically opposite angles with linear pairs. When given two vertically opposite angles like $50^\circ$ and $x^\circ$, instead of setting them equal ($x = 50$), they wrongly assume they form a straight line and write $x + 50 = 180$, solving for $x = 130$.
c7_math_ch05_004	Students often think that lines are parallel simply because they do not intersect within the visible drawing on their notebook page. For example, if two diverging lines are drawn short enough, a student might label them as parallel because "they haven't touched yet." This error stems from forgetting that geometric lines extend infinitely in both directions, meaning lines that form an acute angle will eventually intersect if extended far enough.
c7_math_ch05_005	Students often assume that any two intersecting lines that look "sort of upright" or form a cross are perpendicular, or they confuse perpendicular lines ($\perp$) with parallel lines ($\parallel$). Another frequent error is setting an algebraic expression equal to $180^\circ$ instead of $90^\circ$ when solving for an unknown angle in a perpendicular intersection, mixing up a linear pair with a single right angle. For example, given $5x = 90$, a student might incorrectly write $5x = 180$ because they confuse perpendicularity with a straight line.
c7_math_ch05_006	Students often confuse a line segment or ray that terminates before crossing all lines as a full transversal, or they believe that any line crossing multiple lines is a transversal even if all lines meet at a single common point. For example, if three lines intersect at one single vertex (concurrent lines), students mistakenly label the third line as a "transversal" of the other two, ignoring the requirement for *distinct, separate* intersection points.
c7_math_ch05_007	Students frequently confuse corresponding angles with alternate interior angles or consecutive interior angles. When solving equations involving parallel lines, they often incorrectly set corresponding angle expressions to add up to 180° (supplementary) instead of setting them equal to each other, treating them as if they were interior angles on the same side of the transversal. For example, if given $(2x)^\circ$ and $(120)^\circ$ as corresponding angles, a student might write $2x + 120 = 180$ instead of $2x = 120$.
c7_math_ch05_008	Students frequently confuse alternate interior angles with consecutive interior angles on the same side of the transversal. When solving algebraic problems where lines are parallel, they mistakenly set the sum of alternate interior angles to $180^\circ$ (e.g., writing $(3x) + (2x) = 180$) instead of equating them $(3x = 2x)$.
c7_math_ch05_009	Students frequently confuse interior angles on the same side of a transversal with alternate interior angles or corresponding angles. When given two co-interior angles like $(2x)^\circ$ and $(120)^\circ$, they mistakenly set them equal to each other ($2x = 120$) instead of setting their sum to $180^\circ$ ($2x + 120 = 180$), applying the wrong geometric rule.
c7_math_ch05_010	Students often change the compass radius halfway through copying an angle between the transversal intersection and the external point. For example, if they open the compass to 3 cm to draw an arc on the baseline, they mistakenly adjust it to 4 cm when drawing the matching arc at the point $P$, resulting in intersecting lines instead of parallel lines.
c7_math_ch05_011	Students frequently confuse consecutive interior angles (which are supplementary, summing to $180^\circ$) with alternate interior angles (which are equal). For instance, given two parallel lines cut by a transversal where one angle is $70^\circ$ and its consecutive interior partner is asked for, a student will incorrectly write $70^\circ$ instead of $180^\circ - 70^\circ = 110^\circ$.
c7_math_ch06_001	Students often assume every sequence is an arithmetic progression (grows by addition) and mistakenly apply a constant difference when the sequence actually grows by multiplication (geometric) or by changing differences (quadratic). For example, in the sequence 2, 6, 18, 54, a student might look at the first jump ($6 - 2 = 4$) and incorrectly guess the next term is $54 + 4 = 58$, completely missing that each term is multiplied by 3.
c7_math_ch06_002	Students often assume that rules for adding even and odd numbers apply identically to multiplication, or they confuse the results of operations. Specifically, students frequently state that the product of two odd numbers is an even number because they incorrectly add the terms mentally or think "odd times odd equals even" due to mixing up addition rules ($odd + odd = even$) with multiplication rules ($odd \times odd = odd$). For example, they might claim $3 \times 5 = 15$ is even because both factors are odd and they tried to add them ($3+5=8$).
c7_math_ch06_003	Students often mistakenly believe that adding *any* collection of odd numbers results in an odd sum, failing to recognize that the *count* of odd numbers matters. For instance, when adding three odd numbers ($3 + 5 + 7 = 15$), the sum is odd, but when adding four odd numbers ($3 + 5 + 7 + 9 = 24$), the sum becomes even because pairs of odd numbers cancel out their remainder of 1. Another common error is assuming subtraction of even and odd numbers follows entirely different parity rules than addition, forgetting that subtracting an odd number changes parity in the exact same way as adding an odd number.
c7_math_ch06_004	Students often confuse perimeter counting with area counting when analyzing dot grids, adding the number of dots on the outer edges instead of multiplying total rows by columns or summing the interior grid cells correctly. For example, in a $3 \times 4$ grid, students might calculate $3 + 4 + 3 + 4 = 14$ (perimeter) instead of $3 \times 4 = 12$ (total array elements).
c7_math_ch06_005	Students often confuse the Virahanka-Fibonacci rule by adding the term number (index) to the value, or by adding the *first* and *current* term instead of the *two immediate preceding* terms. For example, given the sequence $1, 1, 2, 3, 5$, a student might try to find the next term by adding $1 + 5 = 6$ or $2 + 5 = 7$ incorrectly, rather than adding the last two terms ($3 + 5 = 8$).
c7_math_ch06_006	Students often assume that different letters can represent the same digit, or that the same letter can represent different digits in different parts of the same puzzle. For example, in solving $AB + BA = CC$, a student might assign $A = 3$ and $B = 3$, turning it into $33 + 33$, violating the rule that distinct letters must represent distinct digits.
c7_math_ch06_007	Students often assume that because a total count is large or a grid is large, any symmetrical or patterned configuration can be achieved, ignoring the global invariant constraint. For example, when flipping signs or tokens in rows and columns, they forget that the sum of all row sums must equal the sum of all column sums, leading to parity contradictions that make certain configurations mathematically impossible.
c7_math_ch06_008	Students often assume every sequence is arithmetic (uses addition/subtraction) and fail to test for geometric (multiplication/division) or squared relationships. For example, given the sequence $2, 6, 18, 54$, a student might look at the differences ($+4, +12, +36$) and get confused instead of noticing that each term is multiplied by 3.
c7_math_ch06_009	When analyzing number tricks with division, students frequently divide only the first term of an algebraic expression by the denominator and forget to divide the second term. For example, when simplifying $\frac{4x + 12}{4}$, a student writes $x + 12$ instead of $x + 3$, completely breaking the algebraic proof of the game.
c7_math_ch07_001	Students often confuse the perimeter or area calculations with the basic structural components of a triangle, or they mix up the labels of vertices, sides, and angles. For example, when asked to name the side opposite to vertex A in triangle ABC, a student might write vertex B or angle C instead of writing the line segment BC.
c7_math_ch07_002	Students often believe that if they draw three lines of any random length that meet at three corners, they can force them to form an equilateral triangle by adjusting the angles to 60° without checking if the compass radius matches the base line segment during construction. For example, when constructing a triangle with a base of 6 cm, students might mistakenly set their compass to 5 cm and draw arcs, resulting in an isosceles or scalene triangle instead of an equilateral one.
c7_math_ch07_003	Students often confuse the compass setting with the total length of the baseline, or they measure the compass radius starting from the 1 cm mark on their ruler instead of the 0 cm mark, which shifts every subsequent arc radius by 1 cm and results in an impossible or distorted triangle. For example, if asked to set a radius of 5 cm, they open the compass from 1 cm to 6 cm on the ruler, keeping the span correct but making a fatal error if they misread absolute distance. Another common error is failing to check if the sum of the two arc lengths is greater than the base before drawing.
c7_math_ch07_004	Students often confuse an isosceles triangle with a scalene triangle when the orientation of the triangle is tilted or rotated, failing to measure or check side length markings. For example, if an isosceles triangle is drawn with its equal sides pointing sideways, students might assume all three sides are different because the base looks unequal. Another common error is assuming that if two sides look visually similar, they must be isosceles, without checking the numerical tick marks or given measurements.
c7_math_ch07_005	Students often look at only one angle or confuse classification by sides (scalene, isosceles, equilateral) with classification by angles (acute, right, obtuse). For example, given a triangle with angles $30^\circ$, $60^\circ$, and $90^\circ$, a student might incorrectly call it an "acute triangle" because they see two acute angles, ignoring the vital $90^\circ$ right angle that makes it a right-angled triangle.
c7_math_ch07_006	Students often confuse altitudes with medians or angle bisectors, drawing a line from a vertex to the opposite side's midpoint instead of ensuring the line meets the base at a strict $90^\circ$ right angle. For example, in an obtuse triangle, students try to draw the altitude inside the triangle from the obtuse vertex rather than extending the base line outward to drop a perpendicular, resulting in an inclined, non-perpendicular line segment.
c7_math_ch07_007	Students frequently confuse the angle sum property of a triangle ($180^\circ$) with the angle sum of a quadrilateral ($360^\circ$) or a straight line ($180^\circ$), but more commonly, they subtract only one given angle from $180^\circ$ when two angles are provided, or they incorrectly perform arithmetic operations like adding the two angles and setting that equal to the unknown angle without subtracting from $180^\circ$. For example, given angles $50^\circ$ and $70^\circ$, a student might write $\angle C = 50^\circ + 70^\circ = 120^\circ$ as their final answer instead of $180^\circ - 120^\circ = 60^\circ$.
c7_math_ch07_008	Students frequently confuse the adjacent interior angle with the interior opposite angles. When given an exterior angle and the interior adjacent angle, they mistakenly add or subtract those two adjacent angles instead of recognizing that the exterior angle equals the sum of the *two remote interior angles* on the opposite side of the triangle. For example, if the interior adjacent angle is $70^\circ$ and the exterior angle is $130^\circ$, a student might try to add $130^\circ + 70^\circ = 200^\circ$ or subtract them incorrectly relative to the wrong vertex.
c7_math_ch07_009	Students often confuse which compass radius corresponds to which vertex when swinging intersecting arcs for SSS construction. For instance, when constructing $\triangle XYZ$ with $XY = 7\text{ cm}$, $YZ = 5\text{ cm}$, and $XZ = 6\text{ cm}$, a student will draw baseline $XY = 7\text{ cm}$, but then mistakenly measure 5 cm from point $X$ instead of point $Y$, and 6 cm from point $Y$ instead of point $X$, resulting in an upside-down or completely incorrect triangle.
c7_math_ch07_010	Students frequently measure the second side length along the wrong ray or measure the included angle from the wrong vertex. For example, when given side $AB = 6\text{ cm}$, side $BC = 8\text{ cm}$, and included angle $\angle B = 60^\circ$, students often draw angle $\angle A = 60^\circ$ instead of $\angle B = 60^\circ$, making it impossible to correctly place side $BC$ because vertex $B$ is not being used as the vertex for the angle.
c7_math_ch08_001	Students often mistakenly apply the rules of fraction addition and subtraction to multiplication by finding a common denominator before multiplying the numerators, or they forget to convert mixed numbers into improper fractions before multiplying. For example, when solving $2\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{3}{4}$, a student might multiply the whole numbers and fractions separately ($2 \times \frac{3}{4}$ and $\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{3}{4}$) or incorrectly add denominators instead of multiplying them.
c7_math_ch08_002	Students frequently multiply both the numerator AND the denominator of a fraction by the whole number (e.g., calculating $4 \times \frac{2}{3}$ as $\frac{8}{12}$ instead of $\frac{8}{3}$). They confuse this operation with finding equivalent fractions or assume that scaling applies to both parts equally.
c7_math_ch08_003	Students frequently multiply the numerators but mistakenly add the denominators together (e.g., calculating $\frac{2}{3} \times \frac{4}{5}$ as $\frac{8}{8}$ instead of $\frac{8}{15}$). This happens because students inappropriately mix up the rules for addition/subtraction of fractions (which require a common denominator and combining numerators) with the rule for multiplication.
c7_math_ch08_004	Students often flip the first fraction (dividend) instead of the second fraction (divisor), or they flip both fractions simultaneously when converting a division problem into multiplication. For example, when solving $\frac{3}{5} \div \frac{2}{7}$, a student incorrectly writes $\frac{5}{3} \times \frac{7}{2}$ instead of $\frac{3}{5} \times \frac{7}{2}$.
c7_math_ch08_005	Students often divide the numerator by the whole number while mistakenly leaving the denominator unchanged, or they invert the fraction instead of the whole number. For example, when calculating $\frac{4}{9} \div 2$, a student might compute $\frac{4 \div 2}{9} = \frac{2}{9}$ (which happens to work here because 4 is divisible by 2), but when calculating $\frac{3}{5} \div 2$, they might write $\frac{3 \div 2}{5}$ which results in a complex fraction, or they might flip the fraction to get $\frac{5}{3} \times 2 = \frac{10}{3}$.
c7_math_ch08_006	Students often invert the *first* fraction (dividend) instead of the *second* fraction (divisor), or they mistakenly multiply all numerators and denominators straight across without changing the division sign into multiplication. For example, when solving $\frac{2}{3} \div \frac{4}{5}$, they might compute $\frac{3}{2} \times \frac{4}{5} = \frac{12}{10}$, which results in an entirely incorrect reciprocal application.
c7_math_ch08_007	Students frequently multiply mixed numbers directly by multiplying the whole numbers together and the fractions together separately (e.g., $2 \times \frac{1}{3}$ and $3 \times \frac{1}{4}$), rather than first converting mixed numbers into improper fractions. For example, when solving $2\frac{1}{3} \times 1\frac{1}{4}$, a student might incorrectly calculate $(2 \times 1) + (\frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{4}) = 2\frac{1}{12}$ instead of converting to $\frac{7}{3} \times \frac{5}{4} = \frac{35}{12} = 2\frac{11}{12}$.
c7_math_ch08_008	Students often convert mixed numbers to improper fractions correctly but then forget to invert the divisor when performing division, accidentally multiplying the two fractions straight across as if it were a multiplication word problem. For example, when solving $3\frac{1}{2} \div \frac{1}{4}$, they compute $\frac{7}{2} \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{7}{8}$ instead of $\frac{7}{2} \times \frac{4}{1} = 14$.
c7_math_ch08_009	Students often invert the *dividend* (the first fraction) instead of the *divisor* (the second fraction) when converting a division problem into multiplication, or they apply the reciprocal to both fractions. For example, when evaluating $\frac{2}{3} \div \frac{4}{5}$, a student might incorrectly compute $\frac{3}{2} \times \frac{5}{4}$ instead of keeping the first fraction as $\frac{2}{3}$ and multiplying by $\frac{5}{4}$.
c7_math_ch08_010	Students often cancel terms across addition and subtraction signs in complex fractions—such as cancelling the 3 in $\frac{2 + 3}{3 + 4}$ to get $\frac{2}{4}$—or they invert individual terms of a numerator sum separately before combining them, violating the order of operations by treating the main fraction bar as optional rather than a grouping symbol.
c7_math_ch09_001	Students often confuse "similar" figures with "congruent" figures, assuming that if two objects look alike (like a small photo and a large poster of the same picture), they are congruent. For example, they might look at an equilateral triangle with $3\text{ cm}$ sides and an equilateral triangle with $6\text{ cm}$ sides and state they are congruent because "they are both triangles with equal angles."
c7_math_ch09_002	Students often assume that the letters in a triangle's name can be written in any random order when stating congruence (e.g., writing $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle QPR$ when the actual correspondence is $A \leftrightarrow P$, $B \leftrightarrow Q$, $C \leftrightarrow R$). This error breaks the fundamental rule of vertex-to-vertex correspondence, leading to incorrect matching of sides and angles in multi-step geometry problems.
c7_math_ch09_003	Students frequently confuse which angles are equal in an isosceles triangle, setting the vertex angle equal to one of the base angles instead of setting the two base angles equal to each other. For example, given an isosceles triangle with a base angle of $50^\circ$, a student might mistakenly write that the vertex angle is also $50^\circ$, leading to a total angle sum of $50^\circ + 50^\circ + 50^\circ = 150^\circ$ instead of $180^\circ$.
c7_math_ch09_004	Students often confuse the side length of an equilateral triangle with its angle measure, attempting to set side lengths equal to angle degrees (e.g., writing $5\text{ cm} = 60^\circ$) or assuming that if side lengths are scaled up (e.g., sides become $10\text{ cm}$ instead of $5\text{ cm}$), the interior angles also increase in size to $120^\circ$.
c7_math_ch09_005	Students often write congruence statements with mismatched vertices, such as writing $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle FED$ when side $AB$ actually corresponds to $FD$ instead of $FE$. For example, if $AB = 5$, $BC = 7$, $AC = 9$ in $\triangle ABC$ and $FE = 5$, $ED = 7$, $FD = 9$ in $\triangle FED$, a student might carelessly write $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle DEF$, completely ignoring that vertex $A$ must correspond to vertex $F$, vertex $B$ to vertex $E$, and vertex $C$ to vertex $D$.
c7_math_ch09_006	Students frequently confuse the "included angle" with *any* random angle in the triangle. For example, if given sides $AB$ and $AC$, students will mistakenly look for or use angle $\angle B$ or angle $\angle C$ instead of the correct included angle $\angle A$, which is formed right where side $AB$ and side $AC$ meet. Another common error is writing vertex correspondence out of order in the final congruence statement (e.g., writing $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle DFE$ when vertex $B$ corresponds to $E$ and $C$ corresponds to $F$).
c7_math_ch09_007	Students often pick a side that is NOT between the two given angles and mistakenly call it ASA. For example, if given $\angle A$, $\angle B$, and side $BC$, students think ASA applies because two angles and a side are equal, ignoring the position of the side relative to the angles.
c7_math_ch09_008	Students often try to apply the RHS criterion to triangles that do not have a $90^\circ$ angle, or they confuse which side is the hypotenuse, frequently picking a shorter leg as the hypotenuse because of its visual orientation on the page. For instance, in a triangle with sides $3$, $4$, and $5$, a student might mistakenly use $4$ as the hypotenuse instead of $5$, invalidating the RHS proof.
c7_math_ch09_009	Students often mix up the corresponding order of vertices when applying CPCTC in complex figures. For example, if $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle FED$, a student will incorrectly equate side $BC$ to side $ED$ instead of side $ED$ matching $BC$ only if the letters align properly, or they will match $AB$ with $FD$ instead of $FE$.
c7_math_ch09_010	Students often assume that because AAA proves triangles are identical in "appearance," they must also be congruent in size. They mistakenly believe that knowing all three internal angles of a triangle uniquely fixes its physical dimensions in space, just as knowing three sides does in SSS. For example, a student might look at two equilateral triangles—one with side 2 cm and one with side 5 cm—and insist they are congruent because every angle in both triangles is 60°.
c7_math_ch10_001	Students often confuse the absolute magnitude of digits with the value of negative numbers, assuming that a larger numeral with a negative sign (e.g., $-98$) is greater than a smaller numeral with a negative sign (e.g., $-12$), or they treat zero as a positive number. For instance, when asked to order $\{-12, -5, -98\}$, students frequently write $-98 > -12$ because $98 > 12$.
c7_math_ch10_002	Students often confuse the sign of the integer being added with the operation sign, resulting in wrong directional movement. For example, when evaluating $(-4) + (-3)$, a student might start at $-4$ and move 3 units to the *right* because they see a plus sign between the brackets, completely ignoring that the second number is negative.
c7_math_ch10_003	Students frequently drop or misapply negative signs when converting subtraction to addition, especially when encountering consecutive negative signs like $-a - (-b)$. For instance, in solving $-12 - (-7)$, a student often writes $-12 - 7 = -19$ instead of changing the double negative to a positive addition $-12 + 7 = -5$.
c7_math_ch10_004	Students often apply the rules of integer addition (such as "keeping the sign of the larger absolute value") to multiplication. For example, when calculating $(-8) \times 3$, they might look at $-8$ and think the answer must be negative because $8$ is larger, but they correctly get $-24$ by coincidence; however, when calculating $(-8) + 3$, they get $-5$, and then erroneously carry over that additive thinking to multiplication, writing things like $(-5) \times (-2) = -7$ by adding the numbers and attaching a negative sign.
c7_math_ch10_005	Students often carry over the addition rule for integers—where adding two negative numbers results in a more negative number—into multiplication. For example, they evaluate $(-6) \times (-4)$ as $-24$ instead of $+24$, treating the negative signs as if they just combine to make the answer more negative.
c7_math_ch10_006	Students often apply the rule "two negatives make a positive" indiscriminately to any multiplication problem containing a negative sign, resulting in a positive product when multiplying one positive and one negative integer. For example, when solving $(-6) \times 5$, they incorrectly write $+30$ instead of $-30$ because they see a negative sign and assume the rule overrides mixed-sign multiplication.
c7_math_ch10_007	Students often believe that swapping the positions of negative numbers alters the sign of the final product, thinking that $(-a) \times b$ becomes positive simply because the negative number moved to the second position (e.g., believing that $(-4) \times 5 = -20$ but $5 \times (-4) = +20$). Another common error is applying the commutative property incorrectly to division, assuming that $a \div b = b \div a$ for integers.
c7_math_ch10_008	Students often apply addition rules to division, mistakenly believing that two negative signs combine to make the result more negative (e.g., thinking $(-24) \div (-3) = -8$ because they treat it like adding $-24$ and $-3$). Another frequent error is ignoring one of the negative signs in a multi-step division or expression, treating the operation as if it were multiplying or dividing whole numbers without tracking the negative polarity of both the dividend and divisor.
c7_math_ch10_009	Students frequently misinterpret directional words in word problems, confusing words like "below sea level" or "temperature drop" with standard subtraction or ignoring the negative sign entirely. For example, when told a diver descends 50 metres from a boat at sea level (0 metres) and then drops another 20 metres, students often write 50 + 20 instead of recognizing that descents are represented by negative integers (-50 - 20 = -70), or they treat the resulting negative value as a positive distance because distances are usually perceived as positive.
c7_math_ch10_010	Students often assume that operations involving negative numbers always result in negative answers because "negatives make things smaller or worse." For example, when observing a pattern like $(-7) \times 3 = -21$, $(-7) \times 2 = -14$, $(-7) \times 1 = -7$, students frequently predict that $(-7) \times (-1) = -7$ or $-14$, incorrectly applying additive thinking (subtracting 7) instead of recognizing that the pattern increases by $+7$ at each step to yield $+7$.
c7_math_ch11_001	Students often confuse common factors with common multiples, listing numbers that are larger than the given numbers instead of smaller divisors. For example, when finding common factors of 4 and 6, a student might list 12, 24, and 36 because they calculate $4 \times 3$ and $6 \times 2$, performing multiplication instead of division.
c7_math_ch11_002	Students frequently confuse HCF (Highest Common Factor) with LCM (Lowest Common Multiple), resulting in students multiplying the numbers or finding huge numbers instead of divisors. Another common error is missing factors when listing them out—for example, forgetting that numbers like 36 can be written as $4 \times 9$, missing the factors 4 and 9 while only checking up to 6.
c7_math_ch11_003	Students frequently confuse factors with multiples, listing numbers that are larger than the given number (e.g., listing $12, 24, 36$ as factors of 12 instead of $1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12$). Another common error is stopping the listing process too early before checking all integer pairs up to the square root of the number, thereby missing middle factors like 6 in the number 36.
c7_math_ch11_004	Students frequently confuse the rules of HCF and LCM when selecting powers from prime factorisation. Specifically, when finding the HCF, they mistakenly select the *highest* power of common prime factors or include non-common prime factors (which is the rule for LCM), leading to an answer that is a multiple rather than a factor. For instance, for numbers with prime factorisations $2^3 \times 3^2$ and $2^2 \times 3^4$, a student might write the HCF as $2^3 \times 3^4$ instead of $2^2 \times 3^2$.
c7_math_ch11_005	Students frequently mistake the final quotient for the HCF instead of taking the final non-zero remainder. For example, when finding the HCF of 48 and 18, they write $48 = 18 \times 2 + 12$, then $18 = 12 \times 1 + 6$, then $12 = 6 \times 2 + 0$. When the remainder becomes zero, they see the quotient 2 from the last line ($6 \times 2$) and incorrectly report 2 as the HCF instead of the divisor 6.
c7_math_ch11_006	Students frequently confuse the rule for finding LCM via prime factorisation with the rule for HCF. Specifically, when selecting prime factors from exponential forms (e.g., $2^3$ and $2^2$), students take the lowest exponent (which yields the HCF) instead of taking the highest exponent for every prime present. For instance, for numbers 8 ($2^3$) and 12 ($2^2 \times 3$), a student will incorrectly write LCM $= 2^2 = 4$ instead of LCM $= 2^3 \times 3 = 24$.
c7_math_ch11_007	Students often confuse the listing of multiples with finding factors, or they stop listing too early before the first common multiple appears. For instance, when finding the LCM of 4 and 10, a student might list factors (1, 2, 4 and 1, 2, 5, 10) instead of multiples (4, 8, 12... and 10, 20...), or they might stop at 4 and 10, mistakenly concluding 4 or 10 is the LCM because they haven't extended the tables far enough to find 20.
c7_math_ch11_008	Students often confuse the rules for LCM and HCF when looking at prime factorisation forms. When asked for the LCM of numbers like $2^3 \times 3^2$ and $2^2 \times 3^4$, they incorrectly pick the lowest powers ($2^2 \times 3^2 = 36$) instead of the highest powers ($2^3 \times 3^4 = 648$), yielding the HCF instead of the LCM.
c7_math_ch11_009	Students frequently confuse the operations when using the formula $HCF \times LCM = a \times b$. When asked to find the LCM given the HCF and the product, students often multiply the HCF by the product instead of dividing the product by the HCF (e.g., calculating $10 \times 1500 = 15000$ instead of $1500 \div 10 = 150$). Another common error is trying to apply $HCF \times LCM = a \times b$ to *three* numbers, assuming the product of three numbers equals the product of their HCF and LCM, which is mathematically false.
c7_math_ch11_010	Students frequently confuse when to use HCF versus LCM in word problems because they memorize keywords like "maximum" or "minimum" without understanding the underlying action. For example, when asked "What is the *minimum* length of cloth that can be measured in exact lengths of 48 cm and 60 cm?", students see the word "minimum" and incorrectly calculate the HCF instead of the LCM, thinking "minimum means HCF."
c7_math_ch11_011	Students often confuse "common multiples" with "common factors" or assume that common multiples can be found by simply adding the two numbers together repeatedly without checking both sets of multiples. For example, when asked for common multiples of 3 and 5, a student might list factors like 1, or add $3+5=8, 8+5=13$, producing completely incorrect sequences.
c7_math_ch12_001	Students often assume that the longer a decimal number is, the larger its value (e.g., believing $0.452$ is greater than $0.5$ because $452$ is greater than $5$). They ignore the place value of the first digit after the decimal point (the tenths place) and treat the decimal part as a standalone whole number.
c7_math_ch12_002	Students often align the decimal points vertically as they do in addition and subtraction, or they miscount the total number of decimal places in the product. For instance, when calculating $1.25 \times 3$, they might write down $1.25$ and $3$, misalign or misplace the decimal point to get $37.5$ instead of $3.75$ by treating $1.25$ as $12.5$.
c7_math_ch12_003	Students often line up the decimal points vertically as they do in addition and subtraction ($1.5 \times 0.23$ aligned at the dot), and then bring the decimal point straight down without counting the total decimal places of both factors. For example, they might compute $1.5 \times 0.2$ as $0.30$ correctly by coincidence, but for $2.5 \times 1.25$, they write the decimal point directly underneath, failing to account for the combined number of decimal digits ($1 + 2 = 3$ places needed).
c7_math_ch12_004	Students frequently misplace the decimal point in the quotient when the whole number part of the dividend is smaller than the divisor (e.g., $2.4 \div 5$). They often forget to write a zero in the ones place or tenths place, writing $0.48$ as $4.8$ or dropping the decimal point entirely and treating it as $24 \div 5 = 4.8$, forgetting that $2.4$ is significantly smaller than $5$, so the answer must be less than $1$.
c7_math_ch12_005	Students often shift the decimal point in the divisor to make it a whole number but forget to shift the decimal point in the dividend by the exact same number of places. For example, when calculating $4.5 \div 0.2$, they shift the decimal in $0.2$ to get $2$, but they leave $4.5$ as $4.5$ and calculate $4.5 \div 2 = 2.25$ instead of shifting both to get $45 \div 2 = 22.5$.
c7_math_ch12_006	Students often miscount the number of zeros in powers of 10 or confuse the direction of the shift, especially when trailing or leading zeros are required. For instance, when multiplying $0.04$ by $1000$, students frequently shift the decimal point only two places or add zeros on the wrong side, writing $0.0400$ or $40$ instead of the correct value $40$.
c7_math_ch12_007	Students frequently misplace the decimal point in multiplication or division and fail to use estimation as a sanity check. For example, when calculating $5.5 \times 1.2$, a student might compute $55 \times 12 = 660$ and write down $66.0$ or $6.60$ blindly without checking that $5 \times 1 = 5$, so the answer must be around 5 to 6, making $6.60$ reasonable while $66.0$ is absurd.
c7_math_ch12_008	Students often misplace the decimal point during division in word problems because they forget to scale both the dividend and the divisor by powers of $10$. For example, when calculating $4.5 \div 0.5$, they might divide $45$ by $5$ correctly to get $9$, but when calculating $4.5 \div 0.05$, they forget that $0.05$ requires multiplying both numbers by $100$ ($450 \div 5 = 90$), leading them to write $9$ instead of $90$.
c7_math_ch12_009	Students often convert fractions to decimals incorrectly by dividing the denominator by the numerator instead of the numerator by the denominator (e.g., converting $\frac{2}{5}$ by doing $5 \div 2 = 2.5$ instead of $2 \div 5 = 0.4$). Another common error is failing to align formats before performing operations, such as directly adding $0.3 + \frac{1}{3}$ as $0.3 + 0.3 = 0.6$ without realizing $\frac{1}{3}$ is a repeating decimal, leading to precision loss.
c7_math_ch12_010	Students often look only at the digits of a computed decimal answer and completely ignore the place value magnitude, accepting answers like $15.2 \times 4.1 = 6.23$ or $45.6 \div 0.2 = 9.12$ because the digits match their mental arithmetic without verifying if multiplying a number by 4 should make it larger or smaller.
c7_math_ch13_001	Students often believe that any question containing numbers, measurements, or math words is automatically a "statistical question." For example, they might classify "How many sides does a triangle have?" or "What is 45 kilograms plus 12 kilograms?" as statistical questions because numbers are involved. They fail to understand that statistics requires *variability* across a set of responses, not just numerical values.
c7_math_ch13_002	Students often fail to cross off or check off raw data items as they tally them, leading to missed entries or double-counting. For example, when given a list of 20 numbers, a student might count only 18 tallies because they skipped numbers or lost track mid-way, resulting in a frequency sum that does not match the total data size.
c7_math_ch13_003	Students frequently fail to sort data in ascending or descending order before attempting to find the median. For example, given the data set [15, 2, 8, 22, 11], a student might pick the middle number of the *unsorted* list (8) instead of sorting it first to get [2, 8, 11, 15, 22] and finding the correct median (11).
c7_math_ch13_004	Students frequently divide the sum of the data set by a fixed number (like 2 or 10) or by the highest value in the set instead of dividing by the actual count of observations ($N$). For example, given the data set {5, 10, 15}, a student might sum them to get 30 and then divide by 2 because "there are two intervals" or divide by 15 because it's the biggest number, rather than dividing by 3 because there are three numbers.
c7_math_ch13_005	Students frequently fail to sort the data set into ascending or descending order before attempting to locate the middle value, or they mistakenly calculate the mean (average) when the number of observations is odd. For example, given the data set 10, 2, 8, 4, 6, a student might immediately look at the raw third number (8) or add them all up and divide by 5, completely bypassing the sorting rule.
c7_math_ch13_006	Students often confuse the mode with the mean or median, attempting to add all numbers together and divide by the total count when asked to find the "average" value, or they simply pick the largest number in the data set thinking "mode" means "maximum". For example, given the set 5, 2, 5, 9, 2, 5, a student might calculate the mean (28/6 = 4.67) or pick 9 instead of counting that 5 appears three times.
c7_math_ch13_007	Students often fail to maintain a consistent scale or forget to calculate the value of partial symbols in a pictograph. For instance, if one apple symbol represents 10 kilograms of grain, and a student sees half an apple, they might count it as 5 kg without checking if the symbol can be cleanly halved, or they might completely ignore partial symbols when totalling. Another common error is mixing up the horizontal and vertical axes when plotting categories versus frequencies.
c7_math_ch13_008	Students often read a line graph as if it were a physical picture or a literal map of a route (e.g., thinking a rising line means the road is going uphill physically, or treating the slope of the line as the actual path of a moving object). For instance, if a graph shows distance against time and goes straight up, students might think the object is climbing a mountain instead of moving further away horizontally over time.
c7_math_ch13_009	Students frequently look at an isolated data point or a single statistic like the mode when analysing a real-world data set, completely ignoring sample size and data spread. For example, if a weather station records temperatures of 42°C, 42°C, 42°C, 42°C, and 20°C, a struggling student might state that 42°C is the only important temperature because it is the mode, ignoring how the outlier (20°C) drastically shifts the mean and median.
c7_math_ch13_010	Students often assume that the "mean" is always the correct and default choice for "average" in every real-world scenario, regardless of extreme values (outliers). For example, if house prices in a colony are mostly ₹40 lakhs with one luxury villa at ₹5 crores, students will calculate the mean and state that the "average" house costs ₹1 crore, failing to realize that no house in the colony actually costs close to ₹1 crore and that the median would provide a much more truthful representation.
c7_math_ch14_001	Students often change the compass opening inadvertently while drawing arcs because they grip the compass legs too tightly or apply uneven downward pressure, causing the hinge to slip. For example, when trying to transfer a length of 5 cm, a student's hand slips, changing the radius to 5.2 cm, which ruins subsequent intersecting arc steps and results in asymmetrical figures.
c7_math_ch14_002	Students often change the compass radius halfway through the construction when moving from one endpoint to the other (e.g., using a radius of $6\text{ cm}$ from point $A$ and a different radius of $5\text{ cm}$ from point $B$). This results in asymmetric arcs that do not line up correctly, causing the drawn bisector to either miss the true midpoint or fail to form a $90^\circ$ angle.
c7_math_ch14_003	Students often place the compass point on the vertex of the angle for the second step of drawing the interior arcs, rather than placing the compass point on the two points where the initial arc intersects the arms of the angle. For example, when bisecting $\angle PQR$, they keep the compass needle fixed at vertex $Q$ and swing arcs inside, which just traces concentric circles instead of finding the equidistant midpoint between the two arms.
c7_math_ch14_004	Students often change the compass radius halfway through constructing a 60-degree angle or a perpendicular line. For example, when drawing an arc of radius 5 cm from the vertex, they might adjust the compass width to 4 cm when making the intersecting arc, which completely distorts the equilateral triangle property and results in an incorrect angle measure.
c7_math_ch14_005	Students often change the compass radius halfway through copying an angle between the transversal intersection and the external point. For example, if they open the compass to 3 cm at the first line intersection, they might accidentally adjust it to 4 cm when drawing the arc from the external point, resulting in intersecting lines instead of parallel lines.
c7_math_ch14_006	Students often believe that any shape with straight sides or equal side lengths can tile a plane, confusing perimeter properties with angle compatibility. For example, they might think a regular heptagon (7-sided polygon) or regular pentagon tiles a floor simply because the tiles are symmetrical, ignoring the requirement that the interior angles meeting at a vertex must sum exactly to $360^\circ$.
c7_math_ch14_007	Students often assume that because a polygon is regular (like a pentagon or octagon), it can automatically tile a plane. They fail to check whether the interior angle is a strict divisor of $360^\circ$ or whether combinations of polygons sum to exactly $360^\circ$ at every vertex, leading them to falsely believe pentagons tile the plane regularly because they have equal sides and angles.
c7_math_ch14_008	Students often confuse translational symmetry with rotational symmetry in repetitive wallpaper patterns. For example, when asked to find the symmetry of a brick wall pattern, a student might state that the pattern has 180-degree rotational symmetry everywhere, ignoring the fact that bricks are staggered and require a specific horizontal shift (translation) combined with a vertical drop before matching, rather than a simple point rotation.
c7_math_ch14_009	Students often change the compass radius halfway through a construction sequence—for instance, changing the radius when moving from marking arcs on the baseline to drawing the intersecting arcs below or above the line. For example, if a student opens the compass to 4 cm to find points $A$ and $B$ on the line, but then carelessly adjusts it to 5 cm to draw the final intersecting arcs, the resulting line will tilt and fail to form a true $90^\circ$ perpendicular.
c7_math_ch14_010	Students frequently confuse which construction method to apply when translating real-world constraints, such as using an angle bisector when the problem calls for a perpendicular bisector, or vice versa. For example, when asked to find a point equidistant from two boundary walls (which requires an angle bisector), students often incorrectly construct the perpendicular bisector of the line segment connecting the wall endpoints, leading to completely wrong coordinates.
c7_math_ch15_001	Students often confuse an algebraic expression with an equation. When asked to "solve" an expression like $4x - 5$, they treat it as an equation and try to "find $x$" by setting it equal to zero or inventing a right-hand side, rather than understanding that expressions can only be simplified or evaluated for a given value, whereas equations require an equivalence condition to find an unknown.
c7_math_ch15_002	Students often perform an operation on only one side of the equation (e.g., adding 5 to the LHS to cancel out $-5$, but forgetting to add 5 to the RHS), or they apply the wrong inverse operation (e.g., subtracting a number when they should divide because they see a coefficient attached to a variable). For example, when solving $3x = 12$, a struggling student might write $3x - 3 = 12$, completely ignoring the multiplicative relationship between 3 and $x$.
c7_math_ch15_003	Students frequently apply an inverse operation to only one side of the equation, or they perform the correct operation on both sides but forget to change the sign when moving terms across the equals sign. For example, in solving $4x - 8 = 12$, a student might write $4x = 12 - 8$ instead of $4x = 12 + 8$, failing to use the correct additive inverse.
c7_math_ch15_004	Students often apply the wrong inverse operation or forget to change the sign when moving terms. For example, when solving $x - 12 = 30$, a student might subtract 12 instead of adding it, or when solving $6x = 48$, they might subtract 6 instead of dividing by 6. This happens because they memorize rules mechanically without understanding that inverse operations literally "undo" what was done to the variable.
c7_math_ch15_005	Students frequently make a sign error when transposing a term across the equals sign or when moving a variable term with a negative coefficient. For example, when solving $5 - 3x = 2x - 10$, a student might add $3x$ to the right side but forget to change the sign or incorrectly calculate $-3x + 3x$, or they might drop negative signs when dividing by a coefficient. Another common error is moving terms without applying the inverse operation to both sides simultaneously (e.g., changing $3x$ to $-3x$ on the same side instead of subtracting it from both sides).
c7_math_ch15_006	Students frequently commit sign-change errors when moving variables or constants across the equals sign, or they fail to distribute a negative multiplier to every term inside parentheses. For example, when solving $5 - 2(x - 3) = 7$, students often write $5 - 2x - 3 = 7$ instead of $5 - 2x + 6 = 7$, forgetting that multiplying $-2$ by $-3$ gives a positive $+6$.
c7_math_ch15_007	Students often write subtraction terms in reverse order when translating phrases like "5 subtracted from a number" or "less than". For example, when translating "7 less than a number is 20", students frequently write $7 - x = 20$ instead of the correct equation $x - 7 = 20$, completely ignoring the direction of the subtraction implied by the English phrasing.
c7_math_ch15_008	Students often make the error of substituting the test value into only one side of the equation (usually the side containing the variable) and forgetting to evaluate or compare it with the other side (RHS). For example, given $4x - 1 = 15$ and test value $x = 4$, a student calculates $4(4) - 1 = 15$, sees the number 15, and incorrectly thinks "15 matches 15, so it works," without realizing they must substitute into both sides independently or maintain the strict balance across the equals sign.
c7_math_ch15_009	Students frequently multiply the number of matchsticks in a single isolated geometric shape by the number of terms $n$ (writing $4n$ for squares instead of $3n + 1$), completely ignoring the fact that adjacent shapes share common matchsticks in a chain.
c7_math_ch15_010	Students frequently fail to distribute coefficients correctly across binomial expressions when setting up word problems involving geometry or grouped items. For example, when finding the perimeter of a rectangle where length is $2x + 5$ and width is $x$, they write $2x + 5 + x = \text{Perimeter}$ instead of multiplying the entire sum by 2, or they write $2(2x + 5) = \text{Perimeter}$ and forget to add the width terms inside.
c7_physics_ch01_001	Students often think that science is just a collection of memorized facts found in textbooks rather than an ongoing, active process of questioning and exploring. For example, when studying how a shadow changes length throughout the day, a student might just memorize "shadows are long in the morning" without understanding how to observe, measure, and question *why* the sun's angle causes this change.
c7_physics_ch01_002	Students often think that school subjects like physics, chemistry, and biology exist as completely separate compartments in the real world, just like they have separate textbook chapters. For example, when a candle burns, a student might say chemistry is happening because the wax melts and burns, but fail to realize that physics is also involved through heat radiation, convection currents of air, and light emission.
c7_physics_ch01_003	Students often believe that an experiment is successful only when it proves their initial guess (hypothesis) correct, and that getting unexpected or "wrong" results means the experiment failed. For example, if a student predicts that salt water will freeze faster than pure water and finds out it freezes slower, they might think their lab work was broken. In reality, unexpected results are valuable observations that lead to deeper scientific discovery and corrected understanding.
c7_physics_ch01_004	Students often confuse a hypothesis with a random wild guess or an uneducated opinion, thinking that any statement made before an experiment qualifies as a scientific hypothesis. For example, a student might state "Magnets are magic" as their hypothesis for why paperclips stick to a bar magnet, rather than framing it as a testable, causal relationship like "Increasing the number of wire coils around an iron nail increases its magnetic strength." This occurs because daily language treats "hypothesis" as a synonym for "guess," ignoring the requirement that a scientific hypothesis must be testable, falsifiable, and grounded in prior scientific principles.
c7_physics_ch01_005	Students often believe that "technology always solves environmental problems," assuming that whatever negative ecological impact a scientific invention creates can be effortlessly cleaned up by a newer invention, without realizing that resource extraction and waste generation often cause permanent or long-term damage that prevention is the only way to manage.
c7_physics_ch01_006	Students often think that the branches of science (Physics, Chemistry, Biology, Earth Science) are completely separate boxes that never overlap. For example, when studying a burning candle, a student might argue it is *only* Chemistry because wax is melting and burning, completely ignoring the Physics of heat radiation and light emission, or the Earth Science release of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.
c7_physics_ch01_007	Students often think that scientific progress happens overnight through sudden, unrelated breakthroughs ("Eureka moments") rather than through generations of slow, interconnected additions and corrections. For example, a student might believe that the invention of the electric torchlight had no connection to earlier discoveries about magnets or chemical cells, viewing it as an isolated invention.
c7_physics_ch01_008	Students often think that if an experiment does not turn out the way they expected or hoped, it is a "failed" experiment and of no value. They believe science only consists of successful proofs rather than discoveries. For example, if a student drops a flat sheet of paper and a crumpled paper ball and notices air resistance interferes with their ideal theory, they think the experiment failed instead of analyzing *why* air resistance altered the outcome.
c7_physics_ch01_009	Students often think that environmental challenges like global warming or pollution are too large for scientific principles to address at a local scale, or they believe that turning off a single light switch has no measurable impact because the Earth is so massive. They fail to understand that cumulative individual actions driven by scientific conservation principles scale up to significant environmental protection.
c7_physics_ch01_010	Students often think science is a static collection of absolute "facts" memorized from a textbook, rather than an active, ongoing method of asking questions, testing hypotheses, and revising models when new data appears. For example, they might believe that once we learned about electric circuits in Class 6, every single truth about electricity was fully discovered and closed forever, ignoring how modern research into superconductors and renewable energy constantly updates our understanding.
c7_physics_ch02_001	Students often think that electricity is "consumed" or used up permanently and disappears completely after passing through an appliance, rather than realizing it is converted from electrical energy into other forms of energy like heat, light, or sound in accordance with the law of conservation of energy.
